title: Earth, Weather & Climate: The Big Picture
objective: After this level you can describe how Earth's rock, air, water and life link into one system that shapes weather and climate.
summary: Earth works as four linked spheres: rock, water, air and life. A tree lifts soil water into the sky, and a big eruption can cool the whole planet.

cards.headline: One volcano erupts, and the whole planet can cool down.
cards.body: Rock, water, air and life sound like four separate subjects. They're really one linked system, and this course tours its parts: rocks first, then the air, the weather and the climate. Start by meeting the four.

cards.headline: Four spheres, one planet
cards.body: Scientists describe Earth as spheres. The geosphere is the solid, rocky Earth. The atmosphere is the air above it. The hydrosphere is all the water: liquid, vapor or ice, on the surface, underground or in the air. The biosphere is everywhere life exists, so it overlaps all the others. Four housemates, one house, and nobody gets a room to themselves.
cards.callout: Geosphere: rock · Atmosphere: air · Hydrosphere: water · Biosphere: life

cards.fact: A large oak tree can release about 151,000 liters of water into the air in a year.
cards.context: Its roots take up water from the soil, and its leaves let it out as invisible vapor through tiny pores. That's called transpiration. Follow one drop: it starts underground, passes through a living thing and ends up in the sky. Three spheres, one tree, no passport needed.

mascot.line: If you remember one thing from this level, make it this: Earth's parts are linked, so a change in one reaches the others.

cards.headline: When rock reaches the sky
cards.body: A big explosive eruption blasts ash and gas high into the atmosphere. The ash falls out within days to weeks. The sulfur dioxide gas lingers, turning into tiny droplets of sulfuric acid that reflect sunlight back to space. Several eruptions in the past century cooled Earth's surface for one to three years. The rocky sphere reached up and turned down the planet's thermostat.

title: What Makes a Mineral?
objective: After this level you can tell a mineral from a rock and list the traits every mineral shares, from a set recipe to an orderly crystal.
summary: A mineral is a natural solid with a set chemical recipe and orderly atoms; a rock is a mix of minerals. Ice counts, liquid water doesn't, and there are just over 6,000 minerals.

cards.headline: Ice is a mineral. The water it melts into isn't.
cards.body: Snow on a mountaintop belongs to the same club as the grains in a granite countertop. A glass of water doesn't make the cut. So what's the rule for getting in?

cards.headline: The mineral checklist
cards.body: To count as a mineral, a substance has to pass every test. It forms naturally. It's a solid. It has a definite chemical recipe. Its atoms sit in a highly ordered pattern. And it's usually made by inorganic processes, not by living things. Ice, the solid form of water, passes. Liquid water fails the solid test, so your glass is disqualified.
cards.callout: Natural · Solid · Set recipe · Ordered atoms · Usually inorganic

cards.headline: Same recipe, every time
cards.body: Quartz shows how strict the recipe rule is. Every piece of quartz is silicon dioxide: one silicon atom for every two oxygen atoms, arranged in the same orderly pattern throughout. Purple amethyst, yellow citrine and pink rose quartz are all quartz. Change the color and it's still quartz. Change the recipe and it isn't.

cards.fact: Scientists recognize just over 6,000 minerals.
cards.context: The International Mineralogical Association keeps the official list, and lately it has approved more than a hundred new ones a year. Rocks are simpler: a rock is a mix of one or more minerals. Granite, basalt, limestone and sandstone are all rocks. Minerals are the ingredients; a rock is the dish.

title: Testing a Mineral
objective: After this level you can identify a mineral by its hardness, streak and luster, using the Mohs scale.
summary: Geologists identify minerals by hardness on the Mohs scale (talc 1 to diamond 10), by streak (the color of the powder) and by luster (how the surface shines).

cards.headline: Fool's gold fooled prospectors. A plain white tile would have saved them.
cards.body: Pyrite has gold's color and a metal's shine. Color and shine can lie, so geologists test minerals in ways that are much harder to fool.

cards.headline: The scratch test
cards.body: In 1812, the German mineralogist Friedrich Mohs ranked ten minerals by hardness, from soft talc at 1 to diamond at 10. The rule is simple: a harder mineral scratches a softer one. Glass rates about 5.5, so quartz, at 7, scratches a window. Your fingernail rates a little over 2: it can scratch talc and gypsum, but not calcite.
cards.callout: Talc 1 · Gypsum 2 · Calcite 3 · Fluorite 4 · Apatite 5 · Orthoclase 6 · Quartz 7 · Topaz 8 · Corundum 9 · Diamond 10

cards.fact: The step from 9 to 10 on the Mohs scale is far bigger than the step from 3 to 4.
cards.context: Fluorite (4) is only about 25% harder than calcite (3), but diamond (10) is more than 300% harder than corundum (9). The scale puts minerals in order; it doesn't space them evenly. It tells you who scratches whom, not by how much.

cards.headline: Streak: a mineral's true colors
cards.body: A mineral's color can vary a lot. The color of its powder, called its streak, is far more consistent. To see it, scrape the mineral across a streak plate of unglazed porcelain. Hematite can look black or silver, yet it always leaves a reddish streak; its name comes from the Greek for blood. Pyrite leaves a greenish-black streak. Real gold leaves a yellow one.

cards.headline: Luster: how it shines
cards.body: Luster describes how a mineral's surface reflects light. Opaque minerals like pyrite and galena have a metallic luster: they shine like metal. Quartz has a vitreous luster, a fancy word for glassy. Hardness, streak and luster together shrink the suspect list fast.

title: Quartz, Feldspar and Mica
objective: After this level you can name the most common minerals in Earth's crust and spot them in everyday granite and sand.
summary: Silicate minerals dominate the crust: feldspars are more than half of it and quartz comes second. Granite is feldspar, quartz and mica, and most sand is quartz.

cards.headline: Of more than 6,000 minerals, a few build most of the ground under you.
cards.body: You don't need to learn them all. Learn three, and you can read a granite countertop and a handful of beach sand.

cards.headline: The crust's favorite ingredients
cards.body: Oxygen and silicon are the two most common elements in Earth's crust. So it's no surprise that silicate minerals, built around them, make up the vast majority of it. At the top of the list are the feldspars, which alone make up more than half of Earth's crust. Quartz comes second. A handful of minerals do almost all the work.

cards.headline: Reading a granite countertop
cards.body: Granite is mostly feldspar and quartz. In some granites the feldspar is reddish orange and the quartz nearly white and glassy. The dark flakes are often mica, such as biotite, which is black or brown. Mica's giveaway is that it splits into thin, elastic sheets, like pages peeling off a tiny book.

cards.fact: Most sand is made of quartz.
cards.context: Quartz is common in rocks and hard (7 on Level 3's scale). It has almost no cleavage to wear it down, it barely dissolves in water and it doesn't decompose. So as rocks break down, quartz outlasts its neighbors. A sandy beach is what's left after the softer minerals have given up.

title: Rocks Born From Fire
objective: After this level you can tell granite from basalt and explain why slow cooling grows bigger crystals.
summary: Magma that cools slowly underground grows big crystals (granite); lava chilled at the surface makes tiny ones (basalt) or glass (obsidian).

cards.headline: Some lava cools into stone columns, most of them six-sided.
cards.body: At Devils Postpile in California, cooling lava cracked into columns as neat as a honeycomb. Rocks born from fire keep a record of how they cooled. Here's how to read it.

cards.headline: Two birthplaces
cards.body: You met igneous rock in World Geography: it forms when molten rock cools. Where it cools changes everything. Intrusive rock cools slowly deep underground, and its crystals grow big enough to see without a magnifier. Extrusive rock erupts and cools fast at the surface, so its crystals stay microscopic. Granite is intrusive. Basalt is extrusive.

mascot.line: Keep this: crystal size is a clock. Big crystals mean slow cooling; tiny ones or glass mean fast.

cards.headline: Why slow means big
cards.body: Crystals grow as tiny charged particles called ions travel through the melt and join them. Deep underground, magma cools slowly, so ions have time to migrate and build large crystals. Lava at the surface is chilled so fast that its minerals have little or no chance to grow. Chill it faster still and no crystals form at all: you get obsidian, a natural volcanic glass.

title: Rocks Made of Layers
objective: After this level you can recognize sandstone, shale and limestone and say what each one started out as.
summary: Sedimentary rock forms when layers of sediment are compacted and cemented. Sandstone started as sand, shale as mud, and limestone largely as the shells of sea creatures.

cards.headline: Sedimentary rock covers about 75% of the land, yet it's about 5% of the crust.
cards.body: It's a thin coat of paint over a much bigger building. And every layer of that paint started out as something loose: sand, mud or shells.

cards.headline: Squeeze, then glue
cards.body: Sediment settles in layers, and each new layer presses down on the ones beneath. That's compaction. Meanwhile, minerals crystallize in the tiny spaces between the grains and cement them together. In sandstone, that cement is often silica or calcium carbonate. Squeeze, then glue: that's how loose sand can end up as a cliff.

cards.headline: Limestone: built by sea life
cards.body: Limestone is a different story: sea life did most of the building. It's mostly calcium carbonate, usually as the mineral calcite. In many limestones, the grains are microscopic pieces of fossil shells from sea creatures that pulled lime out of seawater. So a limestone block can be a crowd of ancient shells, packed so tightly you'd never guess.

title: Rocks Remade by Heat
objective: After this level you can explain how heat and pressure turn limestone into marble and shale into slate.
summary: Heat and pressure change rock without melting it. Limestone recrystallizes into marble; shale's flat minerals line up into slate, which splits into thin slabs.

cards.headline: Michelangelo's David is carved from rock that used to be a different rock.
cards.body: The block came from the marble quarries of Carrara, in Tuscany. Marble is never where rock starts. It's what heat and pressure make out of rock that already existed.

mascot.line: People mix this up all the time. Metamorphic rock is changed, never melted. Melt it and cool it, and it's igneous.

cards.headline: Changed, not melted
cards.body: Metamorphic rocks start out as igneous, sedimentary or older metamorphic rocks. High heat, high pressure or hot, mineral-rich fluids transform them. The rock never melts; its minerals rearrange or react into new ones, and it becomes denser and more compact. Think of it as a renovation, not a rebuild.

cards.headline: Limestone into marble
cards.body: Marble forms when limestone (or dolomite) recrystallizes under heat, pressure and fluids. Its main mineral is still calcite, the one from Level 6. Calcite grains aren't flat, so no matter how hard the rock is squeezed, they can't line up into layers. That's why marble doesn't split into sheets.

cards.headline: Shale into slate
cards.body: Now squeeze Level 6's shale. Its minerals are flat, and pressure lines them up in parallel, like a deck of cards pushed square. That alignment is called foliation. The result is slate, which splits into thin, flat slabs, perfect for roof tiles and blackboards. Schist and gneiss are foliated too, often strongly banded.

title: Gems and Ores
objective: After this level you can explain what makes a mineral a gem and what makes a rock an ore worth mining.
summary: A gem is a mineral prized for beauty, durability and rarity; ruby and sapphire are both corundum. An ore is rock whose minerals can be mined at a profit.

cards.headline: A ruby and a blue sapphire are the same mineral.
cards.body: Same recipe, different color. So what turns a mineral into a gem? And what turns a rock into something worth digging up?

cards.headline: What makes a gem
cards.body: A gemstone is a mineral prized for three things: beauty, durability and rarity. Beauty comes from color, clarity and the way it plays with light. Durability means it keeps its polish through years of handling, which is where hardness helps: remember Level 3's diamond at 10? A few gems break Level 2's rules entirely. Pearl, coral and amber aren't minerals at all.

cards.fact: Ruby and sapphire are both corundum, a mineral made of aluminum oxide.
cards.context: Pure corundum is colorless. A trace of chromium turns it red, and it's a ruby. Iron and titanium turn it blue, and it's a sapphire. At 9 on the Mohs scale, corundum is second in hardness only to diamond, which helps both gems last.

cards.headline: What makes an ore
cards.body: An ore is a natural collection of minerals that can be mined and sold at a profit. That's an economic test, not a geological one: every ore deposit is a mineral deposit, but not the other way round. Whether a deposit pays depends on how rich and big it is, the cost of mining and shipping, and market prices. Level 3's red-streaked hematite is a key iron ore.

title: Soil: More Than Dirt
objective: After this level you can describe what soil is made of and name the layers you would see in a soil pit.
summary: Healthy soil is about 45% minerals, 25% water, 25% air and 5% organic matter. Five factors shape it, and a soil pit shows layers from O at the top to bedrock at the bottom.

cards.headline: Half of a handful of healthy soil is empty space.
cards.body: Well, not empty: those gaps hold water and air. Soil isn't just crushed rock. It's a recipe, built up in layers, and every layer tells you something.

cards.fact: A typical healthy soil is about 45% minerals, 25% water, 25% air and 5% organic matter.
cards.context: The minerals are tiny rock fragments, sorted by size into sand, silt and clay; a clay particle needs a powerful microscope to see. The organic matter is the decaying remains of once-living things. Rock, water, air and life: Level 1's four spheres in one handful.

cards.headline: Five ingredients, one soil
cards.body: Soil develops as its parent material, the rock or deposit underneath, weathers. Four more factors shape it: climate, living things, topography (the lay of the land) and time. Where all five match, the soil matches. Change any one, and you get a different soil.

cards.headline: Dig a soil pit
cards.body: Dig down and you'll see layers called horizons. O on top is mostly decaying leaves. A is topsoil: minerals mixed with organic matter, a good home for plants. E, missing in some soils, has been washed out. B, the subsoil, collects minerals leached from above. C is the parent material. Below it lies R: bedrock such as granite, basalt, limestone or sandstone. Bedrock isn't soil.

title: Checkpoint: Rocks and Minerals
objective: After this level you can sort any common rock into igneous, sedimentary or metamorphic and explain the minerals inside it.
summary: Crystals or glass mean igneous; cemented grains or shells mean sedimentary; lined-up minerals mean metamorphic. One quartz grain can go from granite to sand to sandstone to quartzite.

cards.headline: Chapter 1 finale: follow one grain of quartz through all three rock families.
cards.body: It starts in granite, ends up on a beach and can finish as one of the toughest rocks around. On the way, you'll sort rocks like a geologist.

cards.headline: Sort a rock with three clues
cards.body: Crystals you can see, or glass, point to igneous rock: big crystals cooled slowly underground, tiny ones or glass cooled fast. Grains cemented together, thin layers of mud or bits of shell point to sedimentary rock. Flat minerals lined up into sheets or bands point to metamorphic rock like slate, schist or gneiss. Marble is the sneaky one: recrystallized calcite, with no sheets at all.

cards.headline: One grain's long trip
cards.body: Granite is part quartz. As granite breaks down, its tough quartz outlasts the other minerals and becomes sand. Buried, compacted and cemented, that sand becomes sandstone. Now add heat and pressure: the sandstone recrystallizes into quartzite, a metamorphic rock. Same grain, three rock families.

mascot.line: This is Levels 4, 6 and 7 working together. If you can tell this grain's story, you've got the chapter.

cards.fact: Quartzite breaks through its sand grains, not around them.
cards.context: In quartzite the grains are welded so well that a crack cuts straight through them and leaves a smooth surface, not a gritty one. It's also extremely resistant to weathering, so it often stands up as hills after softer rock has worn away.

title: The Heat Inside the Earth
objective: After this level you can explain where Earth's inner heat comes from and why it keeps the planet active.
summary: Earth's inside is hot from leftover formation heat, radioactive decay (about half) and a freezing core. Convection carries that heat up and keeps the plates moving.

cards.headline: Dig down a kilometer and the rock gets about 25 °C hotter.
cards.body: That heat isn't a leftover curiosity. It's the engine behind this whole chapter: moving plates, earthquakes and volcanoes. So where does it come from, and how does it get out?

cards.headline: Three sources of heat
cards.body: Earth's inner heat comes from three places. Some is left over from when the planet formed. Some is made fresh as radioactive elements in the rock decay. And some is released deep in the core, as liquid iron slowly freezes onto the solid inner core. Think of a pie just out of the oven that also has a few tiny heaters baked into the filling.

cards.fact: About half of Earth's inner heat comes from radioactive decay.
cards.context: Physicists showed it in 2011 by catching geoneutrinos, ghostly particles given off when uranium and thorium decay. Their detector, KamLAND, is a tank of about 1,000 tonnes of mineral oil buried deep underground in Japan. The rest is likely heat left over from Earth's formation. The planet is still living partly on its savings.

cards.headline: Heat on the move
cards.body: The heat escapes by convection, like soup simmering in a pot. Mantle rock near the hot core warms and rises, very slowly, while cooler rock sinks. You met this in World Geography as the force behind moving plates. Rising hot material feeds plate boundaries and hotspots, and cool slabs sink back down where plates dive under each other. No escaping heat, no moving plates.

title: Three Ways Plates Meet
objective: After this level you can name divergent, convergent and transform plate boundaries and give a real example of each.
summary: Divergent boundaries make crust, transform boundaries neither make nor destroy it, and convergent ones come in three kinds: ocean-continent, ocean-ocean, continent-continent.

cards.headline: In Iceland, two plates are pulling a valley open.
cards.body: At Þingvellir, the North American and Eurasian plates break apart, and the land between them sinks into a rift, spreading about 2 cm a year. That's one way plates meet. There are two others, and one of them comes in three kinds.

cards.headline: Pulling apart, sliding past
cards.body: You met the three boundary types in World Geography. Here's the next layer: what each does to the crust. At a divergent boundary, plates move apart and magma pushing up from the mantle makes new crust. At a transform boundary, plates slide sideways past each other, and crust is neither made nor destroyed. California's San Andreas Fault is one; Level 16 takes you there.

title: Hotspots: Hawaii and Yellowstone
objective: After this level you can explain what a hotspot is and why it leaves a chain of volcanoes as a plate moves over it.
summary: A hotspot stays roughly put while a plate slides over it, so it leaves a line of volcanoes: the Hawaiian-Emperor chain, with its bend, and Yellowstone's trail across Idaho.

cards.headline: Slide a sheet of paper over a candle and you get a line of scorch marks.
cards.body: Now swap the candle for a hotspot, a deep source of heat that stays put, and the paper for a moving plate. The scorch marks are volcanoes. Earth has several of these lines, and one runs right under a US national park.

cards.headline: Wilson's idea
cards.body: In 1963 the Canadian geophysicist J. Tuzo Wilson suggested that the Hawaiian chain formed as the Pacific Plate moved over a deep, stationary hotspot. A volcano grows while it sits over the heat, then gets carried away and dies. That's why each island or seamount in the chain is older toward the northwest. The line of volcanoes is a diary of the plate's journey.

cards.fact: The Hawaiian-Emperor chain has a sharp 60° bend, about 47 million years old.
cards.context: Past the bend, the chain carries on as the older Emperor chain, mostly drowned seamounts. For decades scientists argued: did the Pacific Plate change direction, or did the hotspot itself drift? A 2017 study concluded it took both. Even a 'stationary' hotspot can wander a little.

cards.headline: Yellowstone: a hotspot under a continent
cards.body: The same trick works on land. The North American Plate has been moving west-southwest over the Yellowstone hotspot, leaving a trail of volcanic fields across southern Idaho's Snake River Plain. The farther southwest you go, the older they get; the oldest, about 17 million years old, lie in northern Nevada and southern Oregon. Yellowstone's geysers and hot springs are the hotspot's current address.

title: Faults: Where Rock Breaks
objective: After this level you can tell normal, reverse and strike-slip faults apart by which way the rock moves.
summary: Faults are named by how the rock moves: the hanging wall drops on a normal fault (stretching), rides up on a reverse or thrust fault (squeezing), and the blocks slide sideways on a strike-slip fault.

cards.headline: Every fault is a crack, but the rock on it can move three ways.
cards.body: A fault is a fracture between two blocks of rock that move past each other. Which way they move tells you whether the crust there is being stretched, squeezed or slid sideways. Learn the three motions and a broken cliff becomes a clue.

cards.headline: Hanging wall, footwall
cards.body: Most faults are tilted. Picture a tunnel dug along one: the block over your head is the hanging wall, and the block under your feet is the footwall. On a normal fault, the hanging wall slides down. That happens where the crust is being stretched. The Basin and Range of the western US is a whole region of them: blocks left high became ranges, and blocks that dropped became basins.

cards.headline: Squeezed, then sheared
cards.body: On a reverse fault, the hanging wall moves up and over the footwall. That's what squeezing does, and it's common in mountain ranges and where plates converge. A thrust fault is a reverse fault tilted less than 45°. On a strike-slip fault, there's no up or down to speak of: the blocks slide past each other sideways. The San Andreas is one.

title: Seismic Waves
objective: After this level you can tell P waves, S waves and surface waves apart and say which kind does the most damage.
summary: Quakes send out fast P waves, slower S waves and slowest surface waves. The P waves come first; the S and surface waves do the damage, and early warning uses the gap.

cards.headline: In an earthquake, the first jolt is a warning shot.
cards.body: A quake sends out several kinds of waves at once. They travel at different speeds, so they reach you one after another, and they shake the ground in different ways. Knowing the order can buy you a few seconds.

cards.headline: P waves: first to arrive
cards.body: P waves are compression waves: they squeeze and stretch the rock in the direction they travel, like a push passed along a Slinky. At 5 or 6 km per second, they're the fastest seismic waves, and they pass through solid rock and liquid alike. They're the first to shake a building, but they aren't the ones that do the damage.

cards.headline: S waves and surface waves: the damage
cards.body: S waves are shear waves. They shake the rock side to side, across their direction of travel, at about 3 km per second, and they can't pass through liquid. Surface waves come last and slowest: Rayleigh waves roll the ground, Love waves shake it sideways, and both can be very large. Buildings handle an up-and-down jolt better than a sideways shove, so S and surface waves do the damage.

mascot.line: Common mix-up: early warning isn't prediction. The quake has already started; you just hear about it before the shaking arrives.

cards.fact: P waves travel almost twice as fast as the damaging S waves and surface waves.
cards.context: ShakeAlert, the USGS early warning system for California, Oregon and Washington, uses that head start. Sensors catch the P waves, and an alert can reach people farther away before the strong shaking does. It isn't prediction: the quake has already begun.

title: The San Andreas Fault
objective: After this level you can describe the plate boundary running through California and why it builds up large quakes.
summary: Along the San Andreas, locked sections bend rock and store strain until it snaps back in great quakes like 1906; a creeping section slips steadily with only small ones.

cards.headline: In 1906, a fence across the San Andreas was suddenly offset by about 2.6 m.
cards.body: The two halves of the fence ended up about 2.6 m apart. How the ground stored up that jump explains how this fault makes earthquakes.

cards.headline: A plate boundary on land
cards.body: The San Andreas runs about 1,300 km through California. Along it, the Pacific Plate grinds northwest past the North American Plate. The plates never stop, but much of the fault doesn't move for long stretches: it's locked. The locked sections have produced great quakes, including the magnitude 7.9 Fort Tejon earthquake of 1857 and the 7.9 San Francisco earthquake of 1906.

cards.headline: Bend, then snap
cards.body: After 1906, Henry Fielding Reid studied how the ground had moved and proposed elastic rebound. While a fault is locked, the moving plates slowly bend the rock beside it, so gently, over many miles, that only precise instruments can see it; diagrams draw it as a fence bent into an S shape. The rock stores that strain like a bent ruler. When the fault finally slips, the rock snaps back all at once. That snap is the earthquake. In 1906 more than 400 km of the fault slipped.

title: Why the Same Quake Shakes Unevenly
objective: After this level you can explain how distance, depth and soft ground, including liquefaction, change how hard a place shakes.
summary: A quake has one magnitude but many intensities. Distance, depth and the ground underfoot change the shaking, and loose, wet ground can liquefy.

cards.headline: In 1989, one San Francisco neighborhood was hit hard by what lay beneath it.
cards.body: The Loma Prieta earthquake (magnitude 6.9) was centered near Loma Prieta peak, south of the city. Yet the Marina district was particularly hard hit, because it was built on filled land of loose, sandy soil. Distance from the quake isn't the whole story.

mascot.line: People mix these up all the time. Magnitude is the quake's size. Intensity is how hard it shakes where you are.

cards.headline: One magnitude, many intensities
cards.body: A quake has one magnitude: its size. The shaking it causes, called intensity, has many values, one for each place. In the US, intensity is rated on the Modified Mercalli scale, in Roman numerals like VI or X. It depends most of all on how far you are from the part of the fault that ruptured.

cards.headline: Depth and ground
cards.body: Depth matters too. The Northridge quake near Los Angeles (magnitude 6.7) started 3 to 11 miles down. The Nisqually quake near Seattle (6.8) started 30 to 36 miles down. The smaller, shallower one shook harder and over a wider area. Then there's the ground under you: bedrock shakes the least, and soft mud the most, like a bowl of jelly on a bumped table.

cards.headline: When the ground acts like liquid
cards.body: Shake loose, water-logged sediment hard enough and it loses its strength. That's liquefaction, and you've felt a tiny version: wiggle your toes in wet sand at the beach and they sink. Sand and water can even bubble up as sand boils. In 1989, liquefied soil beneath the Marina caused major sinking, cracking and sliding of the ground.

title: Shield, Cone and Stratovolcano
objective: After this level you can tell the three main kinds of volcano apart and link each one to runny or sticky magma.
summary: Silica makes magma sticky. Runny, low-silica basalt builds broad shields like Mauna Loa; cinders build cones like Paricutin; sticky, gassy magma builds steep stratovolcanoes like Fuji.

cards.headline: Earth's largest active volcano is a broad, gentle dome, not a steep cone.
cards.body: That's Mauna Loa in Hawaii. Mount Fuji and Mount St. Helens, meanwhile, rise as steep, symmetrical cones. Why the different shapes? It comes down to how runny the magma is.

cards.headline: Runny or sticky
cards.body: Viscosity is a lava's resistance to flow: thin and runny, or thick and sticky. The key ingredient is silica. The more silica, the longer and more tangled its molecular chains, like a pot of spaghetti. Gas escapes easily from runny magma, the way bubbles spatter out of simmering jam; in sticky magma it gets trapped. So low-silica basalt is runny and erupts quietly, and high-silica magma tends to explode.

title: Lava, Ash and Pyroclastic Flows
objective: After this level you can name what an eruption releases and explain why pyroclastic flows are the deadliest.
summary: Eruptions release slow lava, hard glassy ash and gas (mostly water vapor). The deadliest product is the pyroclastic flow, a fast, scorching avalanche of rock and gas.

cards.headline: The lava is usually the least of your worries.
cards.body: Most lava flows move slowly enough to get out of the way. An eruption releases much more: ash, gas and, most dangerous of all, pyroclastic flows. Here's what comes out, and why the fastest one is the deadliest.

cards.headline: Lava: slow but unstoppable
cards.body: Because most lava flows move slowly, they rarely kill anyone directly. But everything that can't move is knocked over, buried or set on fire. Lava can bury homes and farmland under tens of meters of rock. You can walk away from lava; your house can't.

cards.headline: Ash and gas
cards.body: Volcanic ash isn't soft like ash from a campfire. It's jagged bits of rock, minerals and volcanic glass smaller than 2 mm: hard, abrasive, and carried by wind for thousands of miles. The gas is mostly harmless water vapor, plus carbon dioxide and sulfur dioxide. Remember Level 1? That sulfur dioxide can form droplets high in the sky that reflect sunlight and cool the planet.

cards.headline: Pyroclastic flows: the deadliest
cards.body: A pyroclastic flow is a hot mix of lava blocks, pumice, ash and gas that races across the ground, typically faster than 80 km per hour, at 200 to 700 °C. It knocks down, buries or carries away nearly everything in its path. That's why it's considered the deadliest volcano hazard. In 1902, one from Mount Pelée destroyed the town of Saint-Pierre on Martinique.

title: How Rock Falls Apart
objective: After this level you can explain how frost, roots and slightly acidic rain break solid rock down through weathering.
summary: Weathering breaks rock down where it sits. Ice and roots wedge cracks apart; carbonic acid in rain and soil water turns feldspar into clay and rusts iron minerals, while quartz barely changes.

cards.headline: Water, one of the softest things around, can split solid rock.
cards.body: No hammer needed: just a crack, a cold night and a lot of patience. Rock looks permanent, but at Earth's surface it is always slowly coming apart. Here's how.

mascot.line: People mix these up all the time. Weathering breaks rock where it sits; erosion is the moving van that hauls the pieces away.

cards.headline: Break it where it sits
cards.body: You met the two jobs in World Geography: weathering breaks rock down, erosion carries it off. This whole level is the first job. Weathering happens in place, at or near the surface, and it comes in two kinds. Mechanical weathering breaks rock into smaller pieces. Chemical weathering changes the minerals themselves.

cards.headline: Wedges of ice and roots
cards.body: Rain seeps into a crack and freezes overnight. Ice takes up about 9% more room than the water did, so it shoves the crack wider, like a wedge. It thaws, water trickles deeper, and it freezes again. That's frost wedging, and it works best where temperatures swing across freezing again and again. Plant roots do the same job more slowly: they creep into cracks and pry the rock apart as they grow.

cards.headline: Rain with a bite
cards.body: Carbon dioxide dissolves in water and makes a weak acid, carbonic acid. Soil holds far more carbon dioxide than air, so water seeping through soil gets more acidic still. That mild acid goes to work on minerals. It turns feldspar, the crust's most common mineral, into soft clay. Iron-bearing minerals rust, which is why weathered basalt turns reddish. Quartz? It is very resistant, and barely changes.

title: How Caves and Sinkholes Form
objective: After this level you can explain how slightly acidic groundwater dissolves limestone into caves, stalactites and sinkholes.
summary: Acidic groundwater dissolves limestone into caves. Dripping water leaves calcite as stalactites and stalagmites; sinkholes form where hollows underground settle or collapse.

cards.headline: Under Kentucky, water has hollowed out over 400 miles of cave.
cards.body: That's Mammoth Cave, the longest known cave system in the world. No digging machine carved it. Water did it, by slowly dissolving the limestone with a weak acid.

cards.headline: Acid meets limestone
cards.body: Remember Level 21's carbonic acid? Water picks up most of its carbon dioxide in the soil, then keeps seeping down until it reaches limestone, the calcite rock that Level 6 showed is built from shells. The acidic water slips through cracks and weak spots and dissolves the rock, widening them into passages and, given time, caves. Caves, sinking streams and sinkholes together make a landscape called karst.

mascot.line: A trick for the mix-up: stalaCtites hang from the Ceiling, stalaGmites grow up from the Ground.

cards.headline: Building it back, drop by drop
cards.body: Caves don't only dissolve; they decorate. A drop of water hanging from the ceiling loses carbon dioxide into the cave air and leaves a little calcite behind. Drop after drop, that builds a thin, hollow stone tube called a soda straw, the simplest stalactite. Stalactites hang from the ceiling; stalagmites rise from the floor below. Give them long enough and the two meet in a column.

cards.headline: When the ground gives way
cards.body: Sinkholes form where groundwater dissolves rock underground: limestone, but also salt and gypsum. Some sink slowly as the ground settles into the growing hollow. Others, called cover-collapse sinkholes, can open abruptly, over a matter of hours, when the roof over a hidden cavity finally gives way.

title: How Rivers Carve Valleys
objective: After this level you can explain how a river erodes, carries and drops sediment, cutting V-shaped valleys and meanders.
summary: Rivers carry bed, suspended and dissolved loads, dropping grains as they slow. They cut V-shaped valleys, and meanders erode outer banks, build inner ones and leave oxbow lakes.

cards.headline: A river's bends keep moving, and some get left behind as lakes.
cards.body: Those stranded loops are called oxbow lakes. Rivers don't just flow through a landscape; they rework it as they go. To see how, follow what a river carries and where it drops it.

cards.headline: What a river carries
cards.body: Level 21's weathering hands a river its raw material, and the river moves it three ways. Big grains are pushed, or bounce, along the bottom as bed load. Smaller particles ride in the water as suspended load. And dissolved minerals travel invisibly as the dissolved load, on average about 15% of everything a river carries. How fast the water flows decides what it can move. Slow it down, and it drops what it can no longer carry.

cards.headline: Cutting a V
cards.body: A stream erodes mostly downward, deepening its own bed. That's why a valley cut by a river has a V-shaped cross-section. Glaciers work differently: they are wider, and they scour their sides as well as their floors, so they turn V valleys into U's. Level 25 follows the ice.

cards.headline: Bends on the move
cards.body: Rivers also swing into bends called meanders. Around each bend, water runs fastest on the outside, wearing away the outer bank, and slowest on the inside, where silt and sediment pile up. Eventually the river may cut straight through the narrow neck of a loop to shorten its course. The abandoned loop becomes an oxbow lake, named for the U-shaped collar on an ox's neck.

title: How Rivers Build New Land
objective: After this level you can explain how floodplains and deltas form where a river slows down and drops its load.
summary: Slowing floodwater drops coarse grains as levees and fine silt across the floodplain. At its mouth a river builds a delta; cut off its sediment, as on the Nile, and the delta shrinks.

cards.headline: Some of the world's richest farmland was delivered by floods.
cards.body: Ancient Egypt grew up on the Nile's floodplain. The same rivers that carry land away upstream build new land downstream. The whole trick is slowing down.

cards.headline: A flood's delivery
cards.body: Level 23 ended with a rule: slow water drops its load. A flood puts it to work. When a river overtops its banks and spreads across its floodplain, the flat land beside it, the water slows sharply. The coarsest grains drop first, right beside the channel, building low ridges called natural levees. Finer silt and clay settle farther out. Flood after flood, that nutrient-rich silt makes floodplains very fertile farmland.

cards.headline: Building at the mouth
cards.body: The biggest slowdown comes at a river's mouth. The current fades, the sediment falls to the bottom, and a delta grows. As it builds out, the river splits into smaller branching channels called distributaries. The name comes from the triangle-shaped Greek letter delta (Δ), the shape of the Nile's delta. Not every delta keeps that shape: the Mississippi builds a bird's-foot.

cards.fact: The Nile delta is shrinking.
cards.context: A delta grows only while sediment keeps arriving. On the Nile, the Aswan High Dam and other river management now hold back the sediment that once reached the coast, and the coast is eroding. Cut the supply and the land retreats.

title: How Glaciers Sculpt Mountains
objective: After this level you can explain how moving ice carves U-shaped valleys, cirques and fjords.
summary: Glaciers pluck and abrade rock into U-shaped valleys. Cirques eating into a peak leave arêtes and horns; fjords are glacial valleys the sea flooded after the ice melted.

cards.headline: In Norway, the sea fills valleys more than a kilometer deep.
cards.body: The Sognefjord reaches 1,308 m down. No river dug that. Glaciers carved the valley, then the sea moved in. Here's how moving ice sculpts a mountain.

cards.headline: Pluck and scrape
cards.body: A glacier erodes in two ways. In plucking, the ice freezes onto the bedrock and pulls pieces away as it moves. In abrasion, rocks frozen into the base of the ice grind across the bedrock, polishing it and cutting long grooves called striations. And unlike Level 23's river, a glacier scours its walls as well as its floor. What it leaves is a flat-bottomed, steep-walled U-shaped valley.

cards.headline: Bowls, blades and horns
cards.body: High on a mountain, glaciers carve bowl-shaped hollows called cirques, where most mountain glaciers form. When the ice retreats, a lake called a tarn often fills the bowl. Let three or more cirques eat into one mountain from different sides and they leave knife-edged ridges called arêtes, meeting at a sharp peak called a horn. The Matterhorn in the Swiss Alps is the famous one.

cards.fact: Norway's Sognefjord is 1,308 m deep.
cards.context: A fjord is a long, narrow arm of the sea filling a glacier-carved valley. The ice ground the valley floor far below sea level; after the glaciers melted, the sea flooded in. It's a U-shaped valley with the ocean poured into it.

title: How Wind Shapes Deserts
objective: After this level you can explain how wind builds dunes, strips away sand and sandblasts rock.
summary: Only about 20% of deserts are sand. Wind strips fine particles, leaving desert pavement, carves ventifacts and yardangs, and walks dunes downwind by saltation and slipface avalanches.

cards.headline: Only about 20% of Earth's deserts are covered in sand.
cards.body: Picture a desert and you probably see dunes. Most deserts are rock and gravel instead. The wind explains both.

cards.headline: The wind as a vacuum cleaner
cards.body: Wind is good at picking up loose, fine particles, and geologists call that deflation. Blow the fine stuff away long enough and what's left is desert pavement: a sheet of rock fragments fitted together like a cobbled street. Nearly half of desert surfaces are plains of loose gravel stripped this way.

cards.headline: The wind as a sandblaster
cards.body: Wind-driven sand is also an abrasive. Rocks sitting in its path get cut into flat, sometimes polished faces; geologists call them ventifacts. On a bigger scale, desert winds streamline whole ridges called yardangs, up to tens of meters high and kilometers long.

cards.headline: How a dune walks
cards.body: Sand moves mostly by saltation: grains bounce along close to the ground. On a dune, they bounce up the gentle upwind slope. At the crest they pile up until they spill down the steep downwind side, the slipface, in tiny avalanches. Grain by grain, the whole dune moves downwind.

title: How Landslides Happen
objective: After this level you can explain how slope, water and gravity combine to send rock and soil sliding downhill.
summary: A landslide is gravity beating a slope's strength. Water cuts friction and adds weight; undercutting, quakes and digging trigger slides, and burned slopes can unleash fast debris flows.

cards.headline: Debris flows often move faster than a person can run.
cards.body: A hillside can hold still for years, then let go in minutes. Gravity pulls on every slope, all the time. The real question is what finally lets it win.

cards.headline: A tug-of-war on every hill
cards.body: A landslide is a mass of rock, debris or earth moving down a slope. Every slope is a tug-of-war: gravity pulls material downhill, while the material's own strength holds it in place. When the pull wins, the slope fails. Geologists sort the result by how it moves: falls, topples, slides, spreads and flows.

cards.headline: What tips the balance
cards.body: Rain and snowmelt are classic triggers. Soak a sandy slope and the water cuts the friction between its grains; a rising water table adds load, too. A stream cutting into the foot of a slope oversteepens it, and so does digging for roads or buildings. Earthquakes can shake a slope loose. Landslides happen in every US state and territory.

cards.headline: When fire comes first
cards.body: Debris flows are among the fastest and most dangerous kinds: water, mud, rocks and plants surging downhill like flowing concrete, at speeds that can top 35 mph. They are a special hazard after wildfire. With the plants gone and the soil changed, burned ground soaks up less rain, so even a modest storm can set off a debris flow on a steep slope.

title: How Arches and Hoodoos Form
objective: After this level you can explain how uneven erosion of hard and soft rock leaves arches, hoodoos and mesas.
summary: Hard caprock shields softer rock, leaving mesas and buttes. At Bryce Canyon, fins become windows, then hoodoos; in Arches, sandstone fins weather through into arches.

cards.headline: Utah's Arches National Park has more than 2,000 stone arches.
cards.body: Nobody carved them. Weathering and erosion did, by wearing away some rock faster than the rock right next to it. That unevenness is the whole secret.

cards.headline: Hard hats for rock
cards.body: Where a hard layer sits on a soft one, erosion plays favorites. The hard top, called caprock, resists weathering and erosion and protects the softer rock beneath. That's how you get a mesa: broad and flat-topped, with steep sides. As streams cut through a mesa, they leave smaller pieces called buttes, with steep slopes all round and usually taller than they are wide.

mascot.line: This is Level 21 again: frost wedging and slightly acidic rain, now working unevenly on hard and soft rock.

cards.headline: From fins to hoodoos
cards.body: Bryce Canyon, with the greatest concentration of hoodoos on Earth, shows the next step. Caprock protects softer rock below, leaving thin rock walls called fins. Water in their cracks freezes and widens them into holes called windows. As the windows grow, the caprock above collapses, leaving spires: hoodoos. Meanwhile slightly acidic rain dissolves the calcium carbonate that cements the rock.

cards.headline: Arches in the making
cards.body: In Arches, buried salt pushed the rock above into domes, cracking the sandstone into roughly parallel lines. Erosion widened the cracks and left fins. Water seeping in dissolves the calcite that binds the sand grains, and winter ice pries the rock apart. Where the sides of a fin wear all the way through, an opening forms: an arch.

title: How Mountains Rise and Wear Down
objective: After this level you can explain why old ranges like the Appalachians are low while young ones like the Himalayas are high.
summary: Mountain height is uplift against erosion. The young Himalayas still rise over 1 cm a year; the Appalachians have eroded for 300 million years, slowed by rebounding crust.

cards.headline: The Himalayas rise more than 1 cm a year. That's 10 km every million years.
cards.body: They have been rising since India hit Asia, 40 to 50 million years ago. Yet Everest stands about 8,849 m. Uplift is only half the story.

cards.headline: The old giant
cards.body: The Appalachians are the Himalayas' opposite. Continents colliding raised them between about 500 and 300 million years ago, and they've been eroding for the last 300 million. Geologists think their peaks were once far higher, perhaps as high as today's Himalayas. Now the top of the whole range, Mount Mitchell, is 2,037 m.

mascot.line: Keep this: a mountain's height is a race between uplift and erosion. Young ranges are winning; old ones lost long ago.

cards.headline: Mountains float
cards.body: Why does wearing a range down take so long? Mountains have deep roots of lighter rock pushed into the denser mantle below, like an iceberg with most of its bulk underwater. As erosion takes weight off the top, the crust slowly rebounds upward. So erosion shaves a range, the range rises a little, and erosion shaves it again, over tens of millions of years.

cards.headline: What's left standing
cards.body: Erosion doesn't take everything evenly. In the Appalachians' Valley and Ridge region, tough sandstones and conglomerates hold up long ridges, while limestones and shales, which erode more easily, floor the valleys between. It's Level 28's hard-over-soft idea on the scale of a mountain range.

title: Checkpoint: Shaping the Land
objective: After this level you can trace how water, ice, wind and gravity turn rock into the landscapes you see.
summary: One grain's trip from mountain to sea ties the chapter together: weathering frees it, ice or landslides move it, rivers carry it, and floodplains and deltas catch it.

cards.headline: Chapter 3 finale: follow one grain from a mountaintop to the sea.
cards.body: Every level in this chapter was one leg of the same trip. Put them together and you can read almost any landscape.

cards.headline: Down the mountain
cards.body: High up, water freezes in a crack and wedges a chunk of granite loose. Carbonic acid turns its feldspar into clay, but the quartz survives. A glacier plucks the chunk away, or a rainstorm sends it down the slope in a landslide. Either way, gravity hands it to a river.

cards.headline: Down the river
cards.body: The river pushes the big grains along its bed and carries the silt in suspension. Where it slows, it drops them: sediment on the inside of bends, coarse grains on the levees, mud across the floodplain, and the rest at the mouth, where it builds a delta. Mississippi mud comes from a huge area: the river and its tributaries drain about 40% of the continental United States.

title: Hutton Discovers Deep Time
objective: After this level you can explain how James Hutton read tilted rock layers to argue that Earth is immensely old.
summary: James Hutton argued in 1785 that slow, repeating cycles shaped Earth. At Siccar Point in 1788, tilted layers under red sandstone showed him how much time that took.

cards.headline: In 1788, a rocky Scottish point showed that Earth is unimaginably old.
cards.body: A widely held view in Hutton's day was that Earth was about 6,000 years old. One cliff on the Scottish coast gave James Hutton striking proof that it was far, far older. What did he see?

cards.headline: Hutton's big idea
cards.body: James Hutton, a Scottish geologist, watched ordinary things happen: rain and rivers wearing land down, sediment settling in the sea, layers hardening into rock, land being pushed up again. In 1785 he argued that these slow cycles had repeated many times over. If everyday processes built the whole landscape, the age of the Earth had to be inconceivably great. Small changes, repeated long enough, build a planet.

cards.headline: Two sets of rock at an angle
cards.body: In June 1788, Hutton visited Siccar Point with his friends John Playfair and James Hall. There, layers of greywacke sandstone and mudstone stand nearly vertical. Across their worn tops lie younger, gently sloping layers of red sandstone. Where two sets of rock formed at different times meet like this, geologists call it an unconformity.

cards.headline: Reading the gap
cards.body: Sediment settles in flat layers, so Hutton read the cliff as a story in steps. Flat layers formed under the sea. They were tilted on end and raised above the water. Erosion wore them down. They sank again and were buried under new flat layers. Every step is slow, and the whole sequence needs an enormous stretch of time. Playfair called it looking into "the abyss of time."
cards.callout: Laid flat, tilted up, worn down, buried again

title: How Rock Layers Tell Order
objective: After this level you can use superposition and cross-cutting to put rock layers and events in order.
summary: Superposition says the bottom layer of an undisturbed stack is oldest; cross-cutting says whatever cuts through rock is younger. Together they put events in order, not in years.

cards.headline: Rock layers don't come with dates. You can still tell which came first.
cards.body: A cliff is like a diary with the pages glued together and no dates written in. Two simple rules let geologists read its pages in the right order.

cards.headline: Rule one: the bottom came first
cards.body: In 1669 Nicolas Steno pointed out that sediment settles out of water in flat, horizontal layers, each one on top of the last. So in an undisturbed stack, the oldest layer is at the bottom and the youngest is on top. That's superposition. Think of a laundry basket: the shirt at the bottom went in first.
cards.callout: Undisturbed layers: oldest at the bottom, youngest on top

cards.headline: Rule two: the cutter is younger
cards.body: Sometimes magma forces its way up through a stack of layers and cools into a wall of rock called a dike. The dike must be younger than every layer it slices through: you can't cut a cake before it's baked. The same goes for a fault that breaks the layers, and for an erosion surface that wears them down. This is the principle of cross-cutting relationships.

mascot.line: People mix these up: superposition tells you which layer is older, never how many years older. Order first, dates later.

cards.fact: These rules give order, not ages in years.
cards.context: Two layers could have formed a few hours apart or millions of years apart; superposition can't tell. And where layers were overturned, or older rock was shoved over younger rock as mountain belts formed, the bottom-first rule can mislead. So geologists check for signs of disturbance first.

title: Index Fossils: Nature's Timestamps
objective: After this level you can explain how short-lived, widespread fossils let geologists match rock layers across continents.
summary: William Smith found fossils in the same order everywhere. Index fossils, from short-lived, widespread species, let geologists match rock layers of the same age across the world.

cards.headline: A canal surveyor cracked the code of rock layers with his fossil collection.
cards.body: In the 1790s, William Smith kept finding the same fossils in the same layers of English rock. That hunch let geologists match rocks across whole continents.

cards.headline: Same order, everywhere
cards.body: Smith was a surveyor planning canal routes, so he studied rocks up close. He saw that fossils in sedimentary rock always show up in a set order from bottom to top, and that the same order turns up in rocks elsewhere. That's faunal succession. With it he could identify a layer wherever it was exposed, and in 1815 he published a geologic map of England and Wales. Fossils had become a barcode for rock.

cards.headline: What makes a good timestamp
cards.body: Not every fossil helps. The best index fossils are easy to recognize, abundant, spread over a wide area, and from a species that lasted only a short span of geologic time. Short-lived is the key. If a species existed only briefly, any rock holding it must have formed during that brief window.
cards.callout: Easy to spot, common, widespread, short-lived

cards.fact: Rocks far apart that share an index fossil formed in the same slice of time.
cards.context: Fossils record the slow development of life, so geologists use index fossils to identify rocks of the same age throughout the world, even with oceans in between. Ammonoids, extinct sea animals, are among the favorites.

title: How Radioactive Clocks Date Rocks
objective: After this level you can explain how uranium-lead dating gives a rock's age in years and why carbon dating cannot.
summary: Radioactive parent atoms turn into daughters at a steady rate. Zircon takes in uranium but rejects lead, so its lead measures time since it crystallized. Carbon-14 is far too short-lived for rocks.

cards.headline: Tiny zircon crystals carry clocks that started ticking the day they formed.
cards.body: No one was around with a calendar when ancient rocks formed. So how can a geologist say a rock is hundreds of millions of years old? The answer is hidden in its atoms.

cards.headline: An atomic hourglass
cards.body: Some atoms are unstable. A radioactive parent atom, like uranium-238, turns into a daughter atom of another element, like lead-206, at a steady rate. The half-life is the time it takes for half the parent atoms to change. For uranium-238 that's about 4.5 billion years. Measure how much parent is left and how much daughter has built up, and you can calculate how long the clock has been running.

cards.headline: Why zircon makes a perfect clock
cards.body: The trick is knowing the clock started at zero. Zircon crystals take in uranium as they grow but reject lead. So any lead inside a zircon was made by uranium decay after the crystal formed. That's why a radiometric date marks when a rock crystallized from molten rock. Fossils mostly can't be dated this way, so geologists date igneous rock and volcanic ash instead.

mascot.line: A classic mix-up: carbon dating is for once-living remains. Ancient rocks get dated with slow clocks like uranium-lead.

cards.fact: Carbon dating is far too short a clock for rocks.
cards.context: Carbon-14 has a half-life of 5,730 years and is taken up by living things, so radiocarbon dating works only on once-living material from about the past 50,000 years (Chemistry covers how). Rocks millions or billions of years old need slow clocks like uranium.

title: How Old Is the Earth?
objective: After this level you can explain how meteorites and ancient zircon crystals pin Earth's age at about 4.5 billion years.
summary: Earth's first rocks were recycled, but Jack Hills zircons survive from about 4.4 billion years ago. Meteorites and lead isotopes put Earth's age at about 4.54 billion years.

cards.headline: Earth's birth certificate was found in rocks from space.
cards.body: Earth has recycled its oldest rocks, so no rock here reaches all the way back to the start. To find Earth's age, scientists had to look to meteorites.

cards.headline: The missing first pages
cards.body: You might expect to date Earth's first rocks and be done. You can't: Earth's oldest rocks have been recycled and destroyed by plate tectonics (World Geography covered the plates). The oldest things left are tiny zircon crystals from the Jack Hills of Western Australia, about 4.4 billion years old, found inside much younger sedimentary rock. Zircon resists weathering and wear so well that it survives cycle after cycle of erosion and burial.

cards.headline: Rocks from space
cards.body: Scientists assume Earth formed at the same time as the Solar System's other solid bodies. Meteorites, primitive fragments of asteroids, give the best ages for that moment. More than 70 of them have been dated with radioactive clocks, and they formed between 4.53 and 4.58 billion years ago.

cards.fact: Earth is about 4.54 billion years old, with an uncertainty under 1%.
cards.context: The best figure comes from lead. Uranium decay slowly changes the mix of lead isotopes, so comparing lead in Earth's oldest lead ores with the nearly uranium-free lead in iron meteorites, such as Canyon Diablo, times the whole system.

title: The Geologic Time Scale
objective: After this level you can explain how eons, eras and periods divide Earth's history and where humans appear on it.
summary: The geologic time scale splits Earth's history into eons, eras, periods, epochs and ages, with boundaries set mostly by fossils. Humans arrived about 300,000 years ago.

cards.headline: If Earth's history were one day, humans would arrive in the last few seconds.
cards.body: About 4.54 billion years is too big to picture. So geologists slice it into named chunks, like chapters in a very long book. The chapter you live in is brand new.

mascot.line: You don't need the boundary dates. Remember the nesting: eons hold eras, eras hold periods, periods hold epochs.

cards.headline: Chapters of Earth's story
cards.body: The geologic time scale splits Earth's history into named units, from longest to shortest: eons, eras, periods, epochs and ages. The International Commission on Stratigraphy keeps the standard chart. There are four eons: the Hadean, Archean, Proterozoic and Phanerozoic. That last one is the eon of visible life, yet it covers only about the last eighth of Earth's history.

cards.headline: Where the lines are drawn
cards.body: The boundaries aren't round numbers. They are drawn mostly by fossils: where widespread species appear in the rock record or vanish from it, a new unit begins. That's Level 33's index fossils at work. The Phanerozoic's three eras are the Paleozoic, Mesozoic and Cenozoic, meeting about 252 and 66 million years ago.

cards.fact: Homo sapiens evolved in Africa about 300,000 years ago.
cards.context: That puts us in the Cenozoic Era, in the Quaternary Period and its Holocene Epoch. Squeeze all 4.54 billion years into one day and our species shows up in about the last six seconds before midnight. The whole eon of visible life gets only the last three hours.

title: How Life Filled the Air With Oxygen
objective: After this level you can explain how ancient microbes caused the Great Oxidation Event and how rocks record it.
summary: Cyanobacteria released oxygen by photosynthesis. It first rusted the oceans' dissolved iron into banded iron formations, then built up in the air about 2.4 billion years ago.

cards.headline: Earth's air once had almost no oxygen. Microbes changed that.
cards.body: The oxygen in your next breath has a very old backstory. Tiny microbes made it, and the rocks kept a striped, rusty record of the change.

cards.headline: The microbes that made oxygen
cards.body: Cyanobacteria, once called blue-green algae, use photosynthesis to turn carbon dioxide and water into food, releasing oxygen as a leftover (Chemistry covers how). They also build stromatolites, layered mounds of mostly limestone. Some of Earth's first life is recorded in stromatolites 3.5 billion years old, and living ones still grow in Shark Bay, Western Australia.

cards.headline: First, the sea rusted
cards.body: At first the oxygen didn't reach the air. Early oceans held lots of dissolved iron, and the oxygen combined with it to form iron oxide, which sank to the sea floor. Red iron-oxide sheets piled up between silica-rich layers, making striped rocks called banded iron formations. Only once the dissolved iron was used up could oxygen escape into the atmosphere. About 2.4 billion years ago, oxygen in the air rose sharply: the Great Oxidation Event.

cards.fact: Most banded iron formations are older than 1.7 billion years.
cards.context: Their iron oxide is mostly hematite, alternating with chert or quartz, and today they're mined as iron ore. Rust from an ancient sea floor, dug up today to make iron.

title: How Supercontinents Come and Go
objective: After this level you can explain the supercontinent cycle, in which continents gather, split apart and gather again.
summary: Continents gather into supercontinents, split as oceans open, and return as old ocean floor sinks, every 300 to 500 million years. Columbia and Rodinia came before Pangaea.

cards.headline: Pangaea wasn't the first supercontinent, and it won't be the last.
cards.body: You met Pangaea in World Geography. It turns out the continents have gathered and scattered again and again, like dancers who keep finding each other on a very slow dance floor.

cards.headline: A cycle, not a one-off
cards.body: A supercontinent holds the vast majority of Earth's land in one mass. Geologists now see them as part of a cycle: continents gather, split apart and gather again, roughly every 300 to 500 million years. The engine is slow churning, or convection, in Earth's mantle.

cards.headline: How oceans open and close
cards.body: When a supercontinent breaks up, new oceans open between the pieces. But ocean floor doesn't last forever. Oceanic plates eventually sink back into the mantle, a process called subduction, and as an ocean closes, the continents on either side are drawn back together. Then the whole cycle starts again.

title: How Coal, Oil and Gas Formed
objective: After this level you can explain how buried plants and plankton became coal, oil and natural gas over millions of years.
summary: Coal formed from swamp plants turned to peat, then heated and squeezed into higher ranks. Oil and gas formed from tiny marine life buried and cooked, much of it in black shale.

cards.headline: A lump of coal is an ancient swamp forest, squeezed for ages.
cards.body: Coal, oil and natural gas are called fossil fuels for a reason: they're made from things that once lived. Deep time is what cooked them.

cards.headline: Coal: from swamp to stone
cards.body: Coal began as plants in warm, swampy forests hundreds of millions of years ago. As they died, the plant matter piled up and became peat. Buried under layers of dirt and rock, the peat was heated and squeezed for millions of years, turning into lignite, then subbituminous and bituminous coal, and finally anthracite. More heat and pressure make a higher rank with more carbon: anthracite is 86% to 97% carbon.

cards.headline: Oil and gas: from the sea floor
cards.body: Oil and natural gas started mostly in the sea. Tiny marine plants and animals, such as diatoms, died and were buried under sand, silt and rock. Heat and pressure slowly turned their remains into oil and gas. Black shale, a rock made of compacted silt and clay, holds organic material that can generate both, and some gas later moved into cracks and spaces in the rock above.

cards.fact: The Carboniferous Period is named for coal.
cards.context: It began about 358.9 million years ago, and it takes its name from the coal-bearing rock layers typical of that time. A whole chapter of Earth's history, named after a fuel.

title: Checkpoint: Deep Time
objective: After this level you can explain how geologists read rocks, fossils and radioactive clocks to tell Earth's 4.5-billion-year story.
summary: To date a fossil, put the layers in order, date volcanic ash above and below, and match index fossils worldwide. That is how deep time got its numbers.

cards.headline: Chapter 4 finale: date a fossil that can't be dated.
cards.body: A trilobite shell has no useful radioactive clock inside. But the rock around it might. Put this chapter's tools together and you can pin it in time, somewhere between 520 and 545 million years ago.

cards.headline: Step one: put it in order
cards.body: Start with the cliff. Superposition says that in undisturbed layers the oldest is at the bottom and the youngest on top. Cross-cutting says anything that slices through layers, like a dike, is younger than they are. Now you know the order of events, but not yet the years.

cards.headline: Step two: find the clocks
cards.body: Most fossils can't be dated with radioactive clocks. Volcanic ash can: its crystals grew from molten rock, so their clocks started when they formed. Date an ash layer below the fossils and another above, and the fossils are pinned between them. In one example, trilobites came out older than 520 million years but younger than 545 million.

mascot.line: That's Levels 32, 33 and 34 as one team: order the layers, match the fossils, read the clocks.

cards.headline: Step three: match it worldwide
cards.body: If those trilobites belong to a short-lived, widespread index species, every layer that holds them anywhere in the world gets the same age range. Dates like these, gathered from rocks around the world, built the geologic time scale for a planet about 4.54 billion years old.

title: What Air Is Made Of
objective: After this level you can explain why air is mostly nitrogen and oxygen and why tiny amounts of other gases still matter.
summary: Dry air is about 78% nitrogen and 21% oxygen. Nitrogen piles up because almost nothing removes it, while carbon dioxide, only about 0.04%, still shapes the climate.

cards.headline: Carbon dioxide is about 4 of every 10,000 molecules of air. It still matters.
cards.body: Air feels like nothing at all, yet it's a precise recipe of gases. Most of it does surprisingly little. One of the rarest ingredients does a surprising amount of the work.

cards.headline: Two gases fill almost every breath
cards.body: Dry air is about 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen and almost 1% argon. Nitrogen and oxygen together make up about 99% of it, so every other gas has to share a sliver. Water vapor is the wild card: it swings from almost nothing to about 4% of the air, depending on where you are. Take a deep breath: nearly four-fifths of it is nitrogen.

cards.headline: Why nitrogen piles up
cards.body: Why so much nitrogen? Because almost nothing takes it away. Nitrogen is nearly completely inert in the air, it barely dissolves in water, and it doesn't condense into rain the way water vapor does. So it has simply built up. Oxygen got there another way: living things released it through photosynthesis. The air's biggest ingredient is there mostly because it's the laziest.

cards.fact: Carbon dioxide is only about 0.04% of the air, yet it helps set Earth's temperature.
cards.context: In June 2026, NOAA's global average was about 428 parts per million: roughly 4 molecules in every 10,000. Along with water vapor, it belongs to a small club of greenhouse gases that absorb heat, something nitrogen and oxygen can't do. Tiny share, huge effect. Level 47 shows how.

title: The Layers of the Sky
objective: After this level you can explain why temperature falls, then rises, as you climb through the atmosphere's layers.
summary: Temperature falls through the troposphere, rises through the stratosphere as ozone absorbs ultraviolet light, falls in the mesosphere and soars in the thin thermosphere.

cards.headline: A weather balloon climbing past 35 km finds the air warming up again.
cards.body: Weather balloons report temperature, pressure and humidity every second as they rise, on flights that can last more than two hours. Follow the thermometer on the way up and it does something strange: it falls, then climbs, then falls again. Each switch marks a new layer of the sky.

cards.headline: The troposphere: where weather lives
cards.body: The bottom layer reaches up about 10 km. You live here, and nearly all weather happens here, because this layer holds 99% of the atmosphere's water vapor. The higher you climb in it, the colder it gets. The next two levels show you why. For now, remember that every cloud you've ever seen was in the troposphere.

mascot.line: Keep this: the stratosphere warms with height because ozone soaks up ultraviolet light. That one fact explains the flip.

cards.headline: The stratosphere: heated from above
cards.body: Above that sits the stratosphere, reaching about 50 km up. It holds the ozone layer, and ozone absorbs the Sun's high-energy ultraviolet light and turns it into heat. So this layer gets warmer the higher you go. Warm air sitting on cooler air doesn't churn, so the stratosphere lacks the updrafts below it. Passenger jets fly in its lower part partly for the smoother ride.

title: Why the Air Thins as You Climb
objective: After this level you can explain what air pressure is and why it drops the higher you go.
summary: Air pressure is the weight of the air above you. Gravity packs air densest near the ground, so half of it lies within about 5.6 km and pressure falls as you climb.

cards.headline: A weather balloon leaves the ground about 1.5 m wide and bursts at 6 to 8 m.
cards.body: Nobody pumps it up on the way. The air around it does the work, by pressing on it less and less as it climbs. To see why, start with what air pressure actually is.

cards.headline: The weight of a column of air
cards.body: Air pressure is the push of the whole column of air stacked above you. At sea level it averages about 1,013 millibars, or about 14.7 pounds on every square inch. You aren't crushed because an equal force pushes outward from inside you. You've been carrying an invisible sky on your shoulders all day and never noticed.

cards.headline: Why it drops as you climb
cards.body: Climb a mountain and there's less air above you, so less weight pressing down. There's a second twist: gravity pulls the air toward the ground, so the bottom layers are packed the densest. Half of all the air lies within about 5.6 km of the surface. That's why the balloon swells: the squeeze on it keeps getting weaker until it pops.

cards.fact: Mount Everest's summit, about 9 km up, rises above more than half of Earth's air.
cards.context: Up there the air molecules are spread farther apart, so each breath holds less oxygen than it would at sea level. Climbers are not short of air because the sky ran out. They are short of it because most of the atmosphere is sitting below their boots.

title: Why Rising Air Cools
objective: After this level you can explain why air cools as it rises and expands, and why mountaintops are cold.
summary: Air rising into lower pressure expands and spends its own energy, so it cools without losing heat; sinking air is squeezed and warms. On average air cools about 6.5 °C per 1,000 m.

cards.headline: Climb 4,000 m and a 27 °C beach day turns into about 1 °C.
cards.body: Mountaintops are a little closer to the Sun, yet they're colder than the valleys below. Distance isn't the answer. The answer is what happens to air when the pressure around it drops.

cards.headline: Air that spreads out cools down
cards.body: Picture a bubble of air rising. As it climbs into lower pressure (Level 43), it expands. Expanding takes energy, and the only energy on hand is the bubble's own. So it cools, even though no heat left it. That's adiabatic cooling. You can feel it: let air hiss out of a bike tire valve and the escaping air feels cool on your hand.

cards.headline: Sinking air warms up
cards.body: Run the film backward. Sinking air meets higher pressure, gets squeezed into a smaller space, and the squeeze warms it. Dry air cools about 10 °C for every kilometer it rises, and warms at that same rate as it sinks. Up means cooler, down means warmer, with no heater or fridge involved.

cards.headline: Why mountaintops are cold
cards.body: Real air rarely rises dry and alone, so the average drop is gentler: about 6.5 °C for every 1,000 m you climb. That's the standard lapse rate. Start at 27 °C at sea level, and at 4,000 m you'd expect about 1 °C. Pack a jacket for the summit, whatever the weather at the trailhead.

title: The Ozone Layer
objective: After this level you can explain why the ozone layer thinned and how the Montreal Protocol is helping it recover.
summary: CFCs drift up to the stratosphere, where ultraviolet light frees chlorine that destroys ozone. The 1987 Montreal Protocol phased out 99% of these chemicals, and ozone is slowly recovering.

cards.headline: 1985: the ozone over an Antarctic station had thinned by a third.
cards.body: British Antarctic Survey scientists reported that by 1984 the ozone above Halley station was only about two-thirds as thick as in earlier decades. Something was thinning the planet's sunscreen. The suspects were chemicals called CFCs, found in aerosol cans and fridges.

cards.headline: How a spray can reaches the stratosphere
cards.body: CFCs are so stable that nothing in the lower air breaks them down. So they drift upward, taking two to five years to reach the stratosphere. Up there, intense ultraviolet light finally splits them and frees chlorine atoms. One chlorine atom can destroy over 100,000 ozone molecules before it is removed. A small leak, an enormous bill.

cards.headline: The world said no
cards.body: The Montreal Protocol, signed in 1987, set out to phase out the chemicals that destroy ozone. It achieved universal ratification, with 198 parties, and 99 per cent of those chemicals have been phased out. Because the old ones linger, recovery takes decades: ozone should be back to 1980 levels around 2040 across most of the globe, and around 2066 over Antarctica.

mascot.line: People mix these two up all the time. Keep them in separate boxes: the ozone hole is about ultraviolet light, not warming.

cards.headline: The ozone hole isn't what's warming the planet
cards.body: The "hole" isn't a hole at all, but a huge patch of very thin ozone that forms each southern spring. It lets extra ultraviolet light through, and that extra light can't explain the warming of Earth's surface. The hole's role in global warming is small next to the impact of human activities.

title: Why the Sky Is Blue
objective: After this level you can explain why air scatters blue light and why sunsets turn red and orange.
summary: Air molecules, far smaller than light waves, scatter short blue waves much more than red (Rayleigh scattering). At sunset, light crosses so much air that the blue is scattered away.

cards.headline: Stand on the Moon at noon and the sky is black.
cards.body: The Sun blazes overhead, yet the sky is as dark as night, as the Apollo photos show. The Moon has no atmosphere. So Earth's blue sky isn't coming from the Sun alone. It's coming from the air.

cards.headline: Sunlight is every color at once
cards.body: Sunlight looks white, but it is a mix of colors, each with its own wavelength. Red has the longest waves. Blue and violet have much shorter ones. A prism sorts them by bending the light. The air sorts them a different way: by scattering it.

cards.headline: Tiny molecules, picky scattering
cards.body: The air is mostly nitrogen and oxygen molecules (Level 41), far smaller than a wave of light. Molecules that small scatter short waves much more than long ones, bouncing blue light all over the sky. That's Rayleigh scattering. Violet scatters even more, but sunlight has less violet and your eyes are more sensitive to blue. So you see blue arriving from every direction.

cards.headline: Why sunsets turn red
cards.body: When the Sun is low, its light crosses a much thicker slice of atmosphere to reach you. Along the way, more of the blue is scattered off to the side, leaving the reds and oranges to come through. Dust and other tiny particles can deepen the red. Blue noon, red evening: it's the same scattering, seen along different paths.
