title: The Greenhouse Effect, Up Close
objective: After this level you can explain why carbon dioxide and water vapor trap heat while nitrogen and oxygen let it pass.
summary: Sunlight warms the surface, which gives off infrared. Molecules of three or more atoms, like carbon dioxide and water vapor, vibrate in ways that absorb it; two-atom nitrogen and oxygen cannot.

cards.headline: Nitrogen and oxygen are 99% of the air, and they can't absorb Earth's heat.
cards.body: You met the greenhouse effect in World Geography: some gases trap heat like a blanket. This level asks the sharper question. Why do a few rare gases catch heat while the two big ones let it slip straight past?

cards.headline: Light in, heat out
cards.body: Roughly half of the sunlight arriving at Earth passes through the air and is absorbed by the ground and ocean. The warmed surface then gives off energy of a different kind: thermal infrared, the invisible heat you feel from a heat lamp. So the question becomes: which gases can catch that outgoing heat?

cards.headline: It's all in the wiggle
cards.body: Molecules vibrate. A two-atom molecule like nitrogen (N2) or oxygen (O2) can only stretch in and out, and because its two atoms are identical, its electric charge stays balanced as it moves. Carbon dioxide, water vapor and methane have three or more atoms and vibrate in more complex patterns that shift their charge. Those wiggles let them absorb infrared. Nitrogen and oxygen just let it pass.

cards.headline: Heat passed around like a ball
cards.body: A greenhouse gas molecule that absorbs infrared soon sends it back out. Some heads to space. Some is caught by another greenhouse gas molecule. Some goes back down to the surface. That game of catch keeps heat near the ground, which is exactly what the blanket picture was trying to say.

learned: Sunlight in, infrared heat out

title: Earth's Energy Budget
objective: After this level you can explain how sunlight in, heat out and reflectiveness (albedo) set Earth's temperature.
summary: Earth reflects about 29% of sunlight and absorbs the rest. Its temperature settles where absorbed sunlight equals heat radiated away; albedo sets how much is absorbed.

cards.headline: About 29% of the sunlight reaching Earth bounces straight back to space.
cards.body: Clouds, snow, ice and even specks in the air act as mirrors. The other 71% is absorbed and warms the planet. So what stops Earth from heating up forever?

mascot.line: Keep this: energy in versus energy out. Change either side and the temperature has to move.

cards.headline: A budget that balances
cards.body: Think of Earth's temperature as a bank balance. Energy comes in as sunlight and goes out as infrared heat. When the two match, the global temperature holds steady: scientists call it radiative equilibrium. Anything that changes what comes in or goes out moves the temperature. More greenhouse gas, for example, cuts the heat escaping to space.

cards.headline: Why it doesn't run away
cards.body: Here's the brake. As Earth's surface warms, the heat it radiates to space rises quickly. So if the balance tips, Earth warms until it's shedding enough extra heat to match, then settles at a new, higher temperature. That's what keeps a planet from heating without end.

cards.headline: Albedo: how shiny the planet is
cards.body: Albedo measures how much sunlight a surface reflects, from 0 (absorbs everything) to 1 (reflects everything). Open ocean reflects only about 6% of sunlight. Snow-covered ice reflects as much as 90%. You already know this barefoot: dark blacktop on a summer day soaks up far more sunshine than lighter concrete.

title: Why Winds Curve
objective: After this level you can explain how Earth's spin deflects moving air (the Coriolis effect) and why storms spin.
summary: The ground moves faster at the Equator than near the poles, so air moving north or south seems to curve. Air rushing into a storm is deflected, so storms spin.

cards.headline: Your sink doesn't drain the other way in Australia.
cards.body: It's famous trivia, and it's wrong: a sink's swirl depends on its shape and on how the water got moving. But the idea behind the myth is real, and it is strong enough to spin whole storms.

cards.headline: A planet that spins at different speeds
cards.body: Earth turns once a day, but not every place moves equally fast. The Equator, the widest part, races along at nearly 1,600 km/h; near the poles the ground barely moves. Air heading north or south keeps its own motion while the ground beneath it moves at a different speed. So its path appears to curve. No force shoves it: the ground just shifts underneath.

cards.headline: Try it on a merry-go-round
cards.body: Roll a ball to a friend across a spinning merry-go-round and it seems to curve away. Someone standing on the ground sees it roll in a straight line: you and your friend moved out of its path. Earth is the merry-go-round and the wind is the ball. You met the rule in World Geography: air bends right in the Northern Hemisphere, left in the Southern.

cards.headline: Why storms spin
cards.body: Air rushes toward a storm's low-pressure center from every direction. Each stream is nudged sideways, so instead of meeting in the middle the air swirls around it: counterclockwise in the Northern Hemisphere, clockwise in the Southern. The effect is strongest near the poles and zero at the Equator, which is why hurricanes almost never form there and never cross it.

title: Milestone: A Planet Always Changing
objective: After this level you can connect rocks, moving plates, erosion, deep time and the air into one picture of a planet that never sits still.
summary: Earth is about 4.54 billion years old: slow changes like creeping plates and weathered grains add up over deep time, while the air links rock, water and life on a faster clock.

cards.headline: Milestone: halfway to Mastery. Nothing on this planet sits still.
cards.body: You started with crystals and grains of sand and climbed all the way to the top of the sky. Now put the pieces into one picture: a planet about 4.54 billion years old whose rock, air and water are always changing, some of it fast and some of it unimaginably slowly.

cards.headline: Slow, but never still
cards.body: You met plate tectonics in World Geography. The plates creep 2 to 15 cm a year, about as fast as your fingernails grow. That sounds like nothing, but even at 2 cm a year a plate travels 20 km in a million years, and Earth has had about 4.54 billion years. Rock changes the same patient way: remember Level 10's quartz grain, from granite to sand to sandstone to quartzite?
cards.callout: Slow + deep time = a remade planet

mascot.line: It connects: every level so far is one piece of the same machine. Rock, air and water are always passing change along.

cards.headline: Fast, and felt everywhere
cards.body: The air runs on a faster clock, and it never works alone. Earth's spin bends the wind into spinning storms (Level 49). One big eruption can put sulfur high in the sky and cool the whole planet for one to three years (Level 1). Rock, air, water and life keep trading energy and matter, which is why this course treats them as one system.

title: Humidity and the Dew Point
objective: After this level you can explain why warm air can hold more water vapor and what the dew point tells you.
summary: Warm air can hold more water vapor. Relative humidity compares what's there with the maximum, so cooling air raises it; at the dew point, vapor condenses into dew.

cards.headline: Your bathroom mirror makes weather every morning.
cards.body: Take a hot shower and the mirror fogs over, though nobody splashed it. That water came out of the air. To see how, you need two ideas: how much water air can hold, and the temperature where it lets go.

cards.headline: Warm air holds more
cards.body: Air always carries some water vapor, an invisible gas. How much it can hold depends on temperature: warmer air can hold more, cooler air less. That's why the muggiest days usually arrive at the height of summer heat. In your steamy bathroom, the warm air is loaded with vapor. The mirror is cooler, so vapor that touches it turns back into liquid water.

cards.headline: Relative humidity: how full is the air?
cards.body: Relative humidity compares the water vapor in the air with the most it could hold at that temperature. Half the maximum reads 50%. The maximum reads 100%, and the air is saturated. Here's the twist: cool the air without adding a drop and relative humidity climbs, because cooler air can hold less. The water didn't change. The room for it shrank.
cards.callout: Relative humidity = the vapor in the air ÷ the most it could hold

cards.fact: The dew point is the temperature where air, cooled with its moisture unchanged, becomes saturated.
cards.context: Cool air to its dew point and water vapor condenses into liquid droplets. That often happens early in the morning, when the ground cools to the dew point and dew, or frost, coats the grass. The dew point is also a gauge of how much moisture the air holds: high dew points, common in spring and summer, mean very humid air.

title: Why Clouds Form
objective: After this level you can explain why rising air cools to its dew point and condenses on tiny specks of dust and salt.
summary: Lifted air expands and cools to its dew point, and its vapor condenses into tiny droplets on specks of dust, smoke or sea salt. Sun, slopes, lows and fronts do the lifting.

cards.headline: Every cloud needs a little dirt.
cards.body: A cloud looks like pure water hanging in the sky. But water vapor has a hard time turning into droplets on its own. It needs two things: air that has cooled to its dew point, and a speck of dust, smoke or sea salt to cling to.

mascot.line: This is Level 51's dew point again, just moved up the sky. Dew on the grass and a cloud overhead are the same event.

cards.headline: Up, out and cooler
cards.body: When air rises, the pressure around it drops, so it spreads out and cools. Cool it to its dew point and its water vapor condenses into droplets. Each one is only about a hundredth of a millimeter across, so small and light that it stays up in the air. A cloud is simply that moment, happening high above you.

cards.headline: Four ways to lift air
cards.body: Air needs something to lift it. Sunshine heats the ground, and the warm air above it rises. Wind shoves air up the side of a mountain. Winds meeting in an area of low pressure have nowhere to go but up. And at weather fronts, one mass of air is pushed up over another. Every type of cloud in the sky forms by one of these lifts.

cards.fact: Water vapor condenses far more easily onto tiny specks called condensation nuclei.
cards.context: Dust, pollen, smoke and sea salt all work. Most of these specks come from fires over land and from waves over the ocean, which toss salt into the air. Without them, air would need a relative humidity well over 100% before droplets could form. Luckily the air is full of them, so clouds rarely go without.

title: Reading the Clouds
objective: After this level you can tell cumulus, stratus and cirrus clouds apart and explain what each suggests about the weather.
summary: Luke Howard named the clouds in 1802: cumulus heaps, stratus layers, cirrus wisps, and nimbus for rain. Thickening cirrus can signal a warm front; towering cumulonimbus bring thunderstorms.

cards.headline: The clouds were named in 1802 by a London pharmacist.
cards.body: Luke Howard was an amateur weather watcher who saw that the sky's endless shapes fall into a few families. His names stuck. Learn them and the sky becomes a forecast you can read.

cards.headline: Three families, in Latin
cards.body: Howard sorted clouds into three main types. Cumulus means heaped up and puffy. Stratus means flat and layered. Cirrus means high and wispy; the word is Latin for a curl of hair. Add nimbus and the cloud can bring rain, so nimbostratus is a flat, rain-bearing layer. Today the World Meteorological Organization builds 10 main cloud groups on Howard's system, sorted into low, medium and high.

cards.headline: Tall clouds, flat clouds

Nimbostratus is the opposite: a dark gray, low, ragged layer that brings continuous rain or snow. Towering and lumpy means storms; flat and gray means a long, steady soak.

title: Why Most Rain Starts as Snow
objective: After this level you can explain how raindrops and snowflakes grow inside a cloud until they are heavy enough to fall.
summary: A raindrop holds about a million cloud droplets. Outside the tropics, ice crystals grow by robbing supercooled droplets, fall as snow and melt into rain; warm tropical clouds rain by collisions.

cards.headline: That summer shower was probably snow a few minutes earlier.
cards.body: In the middle latitudes, rain usually starts out as snow or ice high in the cloud, even in summer, and melts on the way down. To see why, start with a problem: cloud droplets are far too small to fall.

cards.headline: A million droplets per raindrop
cards.body: To become rain, cloud droplets have to grow more than a million times in mass. Put another way, it takes about a million cloud droplets to make one raindrop. Condensation alone is far too slow to manage that. Something has to speed things up, and in the middle latitudes that something is ice.

mascot.line: Keep this: outside the tropics, a raindrop is usually a melted snowflake. The ice did the growing.

cards.headline: Ice steals from water
cards.body: High in many clouds, droplets stay liquid below freezing. They're called supercooled, and they share the cloud with ice crystals. It's an unfair fight. Water vapor settles onto ice more readily than onto liquid, so the crystals grow while the droplets around them evaporate to feed them. That's the Bergeron process. The crystals join into snowflakes, grow heavy and fall. Pass through above-freezing air below the cloud and they melt into rain.

cards.headline: Why snowflakes have six sides
cards.body: A snow crystal grows straight from water vapor into ice. Its six-fold symmetry comes from the way water molecules are arranged in the ice crystal lattice. That orderly structure is why snowflakes can be considered minerals: solid, naturally occurring, crystalline and inorganic.

cards.fact: In the tropics, warm clouds can make rain without any ice at all.
cards.context: In a cloud whose top is above freezing, bigger droplets fall through smaller ones, collide and merge until they're heavy enough to drop. Strong updrafts let the drops grow big fast, which is how tropical downpours get so heavy.

title: Highs and Lows
objective: After this level you can explain why high pressure usually brings clear skies and low pressure brings clouds and storms.
summary: In a low, winds meet and air rises into clouds and rain; in a high, air sinks and holds back clouds. North of the Equator, winds circle lows counterclockwise and highs clockwise.

cards.headline: On a weather map, a blue H usually means sunshine. A red L means clouds.
cards.body: Those letters mark highs and lows, areas where the air pressure is higher or lower than all around. You met the rule that wind blows from high to low pressure in World Geography. Now look at what the air does up and down.

cards.headline: Inside a low: air goes up
cards.body: In a low-pressure system, winds blow in toward the center. Where they meet, the air has nowhere to go but up. Rising air cools, its water vapor condenses, and you get clouds and often rain or snow. That's why a low heading your way is a good reason to pack an umbrella.

cards.headline: Inside a high: air comes down
cards.body: A high works the other way. Air from higher up sinks toward the ground and spreads outward. Sinking air holds back cloud formation, so highs bring settled weather with light winds. The effect can last: a high that stays put for a long time, called a block, brings long dry spells, and in summer, heatwaves and droughts.

cards.fact: North of the Equator, winds swirl counterclockwise around a low and clockwise around a high.
cards.context: Earth's spin, the Coriolis effect you met in World Geography, bends the moving air into these spirals. South of the Equator the directions flip. It's a handy check on a weather map: the spin tells you which kind of system you're looking at.

title: Air Masses
objective: After this level you can explain why a large body of air takes on the temperature and moisture of the place it sits over.
summary: An air mass is a huge body of air with fairly even temperature and humidity, set by where it formed. Maritime or continental, tropical or polar: its name tells you what it brings.

cards.headline: Some days, the air over your town came from northern Canada.
cards.body: A cold snap isn't made where you stand. Often a huge body of cold, dry air has flowed south, bringing its weather along like luggage. Other days, warm, moist air arrives from the Gulf of Mexico. Meet the air masses.

cards.headline: A giant bubble of sameness
cards.body: An air mass is a huge volume of air with mostly the same temperature and moisture all the way across, and it can stretch thousands of kilometers. It gets its character from where it forms. Air sitting over cold, dry land turns cold and dry; air over a warm ocean turns warm and humid. Then winds carry it, and its weather, somewhere new.

cards.headline: Air masses change on the road

And where cold and warm air masses meet, as they often do over the middle latitudes such as the United States, they form weather fronts and can set off big storms. Those fronts are the next level's story.

title: Cold Fronts and Warm Fronts
objective: After this level you can explain why the weather changes as a cold or warm front passes over you.
summary: A front is where two air masses meet. At a cold front, dense cold air shoves warm air up fast, bringing sudden storms; at a warm front, warm air slides over cold air and clouds lower slowly.

cards.headline: Gusts, a downpour, a sudden chill. Then the sky clears.
cards.body: That's a cold front passing over you. A front is the boundary at the ground between two air masses, and when one passes, your weather changes. Cold and warm fronts do it in very different styles.

cards.headline: Cold front: a shove from below
cards.body: At a cold front, a cold air mass pushes into warmer air. The cold air is denser, so it pushes under the warm air and forces it up, building cumulus and cumulonimbus clouds and thunderstorms. As the front passes, winds turn gusty, the temperature drops suddenly and heavy rain can fall. Pressure switches from falling to rising, and afterward it's cooler and the skies clear.

mascot.line: People mix these up. Cold front: cold air shoves under, storms pop up. Warm front: warm air slides over, clouds creep lower.

cards.headline: Warm front: a slide over the top
cards.body: At a warm front, warm air pushes into cooler air, but it can't shove the dense cold air aside. It rises over it instead. Clouds form in the warm air high above, so the first sign is often high cirrus and cirrostratus. As the front gets closer, the clouds lower and rain becomes likely.

cards.fact: Cold fronts can move up to twice as fast as warm fronts.
cards.context: Warm air has a hard time pushing dense cold air across the ground, so warm fronts crawl. On a weather map, a cold front is a blue line with triangles and a warm front a red line with semicircles. The shapes point the way each front is moving.

title: The Three Cells That Circle Earth
objective: After this level you can explain how rising and sinking air in the Hadley cell puts rainforests at the Equator and deserts near 30 degrees.
summary: Earth's spin splits the circulation into three cells per hemisphere: the Hadley cell makes the rainy ITCZ and subtropical deserts, the Ferrel cell the westerlies, and the polar front storms.

cards.headline: Sailors feared a belt of ocean that could trap ships for weeks.
cards.body: They called it the doldrums. Air there moves mostly upward, so there's often little wind at the surface to fill a sail. It sits near the Equator, where World Geography's Hadley cell sends air soaring. That loop is one of six that wrap the planet.

cards.headline: The Hadley cell, from the ground up
cards.body: The trade winds from both hemispheres meet near the Equator and rise in a broken line of thunderstorms called the Intertropical Convergence Zone, or ITCZ. From the storm tops, air flows toward the poles, then sinks over the subtropics. Sinking air makes the high pressure of Level 55, and highs hold back clouds: hello, Sahara. Each Hadley cell reaches from the Equator to between 30 and 40 degrees.

cards.headline: Why three loops, not one
cards.body: If Earth didn't spin, each hemisphere would have one giant loop from Equator to pole. But Earth does spin, and the Coriolis effect turns moving air, so the circulation splits into three cells on each side of the Equator. Past the Hadley cell comes the Ferrel cell of the middle latitudes, turning like a gear between its neighbors. Its surface winds, bent by the spin, are the westerlies. Last come the small, weak polar cells, where air sinks over the poles.

cards.fact: At around 60 degrees north and south, warm air from the Ferrel cell meets cold polar air along the polar front.
cards.context: Where they meet, air rises and low pressure forms, so the polar front is a hotspot for unsettled weather. Put all three cells together and you get a giant conveyor belt, carrying heat from the tropics toward the poles.

title: The Jet Stream
objective: After this level you can explain why a fast river of wind high above steers storms and speeds up flights.
summary: Jet streams are fast west-to-east winds about 8 to 14 km up, born where warm and cold air meet and fastest in winter. They steer lows across the map and give eastbound planes a boost.

cards.headline: In the 1920s, balloons launched in Japan kept racing off over the Pacific.
cards.body: Meteorologist Wasaburo Ooishi was tracking the winds high above his country, and they carried his balloons far out to sea. He had documented a river of air for the first time: the jet stream.

cards.headline: A river of wind, far overhead
cards.body: Jet streams are bands of strong wind about 8 to 14 km above the ground, blowing generally from west to east. They average about 180 km/h and can top 400 km/h. They form where warm air masses meet cold ones, and the bigger the temperature difference, the stronger the wind. That's why they're fastest in winter, when the gap between warm and cold air is greatest.

cards.headline: The storm steerer
cards.body: Jet streams carry weather systems along, so most storms don't just sit over one place. The polar front jet steers low-pressure systems, usually from west to east. When the jet runs straight, systems move through quickly. When it meanders north and south, they can stall over one region, bringing long spells of rain and wind.

cards.fact: Flying east inside a jet stream saves fuel, so pilots flying west try to avoid it.
cards.context: Jet streams blow at about the height where airliners cruise, so a plane heading the same way gets a boost from the wind at its back. Your flight home might be quicker or slower than the flight out for exactly this reason.

title: Checkpoint: How Weather Works
objective: After this level you can explain how heat, moisture, pressure and fronts combine to make the weather in your forecast.
summary: One storm ties the chapter together: a low steered by the jet stream brings a warm front's cirrus and rain, then a faster cold front's storms, sometimes an occlusion, then clear skies.

cards.headline: Chapter 6 finale: one storm, from the first wisp to blue sky.
cards.body: A low-pressure system is heading your way. Follow it through and every idea from this chapter shows up, in order.

cards.headline: First: wisps, then gray
cards.body: The jet stream steers the low toward you from the west. Warm fronts often form on a low's east side, so the warm front arrives first. Warm air slides up over the cold air and cools to its dew point, so high cirrus appear, then lower, thicker cloud. Inside, ice crystals grow at the expense of supercooled droplets, fall, and melt into rain.

cards.headline: Next: the cold front catches up
cards.body: Behind the low comes a cold front, moving up to twice as fast. Dense cold air shoves the warm air up, cumulonimbus tower, and thunderstorms roll through. Sometimes the cold front catches the warm front and lifts the warm air off the ground entirely. That's an occluded front, usually found near the center of the low.

mascot.line: That's the whole chapter in one storm. If you can narrate this forecast, you've got How Weather Works.

cards.fact: After a cold front passes, pressure starts rising and the skies clear.
cards.context: Cooler air takes over. If a high builds in behind it, sinking air holds back the clouds and settled weather follows. Weather is air masses taking turns, and fronts are the handovers.

title: Inside a Thunderstorm
objective: After this level you can explain the growing, mature and dying stages of a thunderstorm and what drives each one.
summary: A thunderstorm cell grows in its updraft, turns mature when rain drags down a downdraft, and dies when that rain-cooled air cuts off its warm, moist fuel, all in about an hour.

cards.headline: Most thunderstorm cells live less than an hour. Their own rain helps end them.
cards.body: You met a storm's ingredients in World Geography: moisture, unstable air and lift. Now follow one storm cell from birth to death, in three stages.

cards.headline: Stage one: the tower grows
cards.body: It starts with an updraft, a rising column of warm, moist air. As the air climbs, its moisture condenses into droplets, and a cumulus cloud bulges upward into a towering cumulus. In this developing stage there's little to no rain, because everything is going up. Where does that moisture come from? Mostly from oceans, lakes and rivers, but about 10 percent of the water in the air was released by plants, like Level 1's oak.

cards.headline: Stage two: up and down at once
cards.body: The storm turns mature when raindrops grow too heavy for the rising air to hold. Falling rain drags air down with it, making a downdraft, while the updraft keeps feeding the storm. Now both run side by side, and the cloud often towers 12 to 18 km high. This is the most dangerous stage: the likeliest time for hail, heavy rain, frequent lightning, strong winds and tornadoes.

cards.headline: Stage three: choked by its own rain
cards.body: Eventually the storm makes so much rain that the downdraft overpowers the updraft. Rain-cooled air spreads out along the ground as a gusty wind called the gust front, and it cuts the storm off from the warm, moist air it was feeding on. Light rain lingers, then the cloud fades, sometimes leaving just its flat anvil top. A single cell runs through all three stages in about 30 to 60 minutes. The storm doesn't run out of luck; it runs out of fuel.

title: How Lightning Charges Up
objective: After this level you can explain how colliding ice builds electric charge in a cloud and why thunder follows the flash.
summary: Rising ice crystals bump graupel and turn positive; the updraft carries them up while negative graupel stays low. When the charge difference beats the air, lightning flashes and thunder follows.

cards.headline: A storm cloud charges up a bit like you do shuffling across a carpet.
cards.body: Shuffle, touch a doorknob, and zap: a tiny spark. Moving air and bumping ice inside a storm build charge in much the same way, only the spark is lightning.

cards.headline: Ice bumper cars
cards.body: The main charging zone sits in the storm's updraft, where it's about −15 to −25 °C. Up there you get a mix of supercooled droplets (liquid water below freezing), small ice crystals and soft hail called graupel. The updraft lifts the light crystals, while the heavier graupel falls or hangs in the rising air. So they collide, again and again. Each bump leaves the ice crystal positively charged and the graupel negatively charged.

cards.headline: Sorting the charges
cards.body: The updraft carries the positive crystals to the top of the cloud, while the negative graupel stays in the middle or sinks lower. Now the cloud is split like a battery: positive on top, negative below. The negative charge even makes the ground beneath the storm positive. Air normally insulates, keeping the charges apart. When the difference grows too great, that insulation breaks down in a rapid discharge. That's lightning.

cards.headline: Flash first, boom later
cards.body: You met thunder in World Geography: lightning heats the air so fast that it expands with a bang. You see the flash almost at once, but the sound needs about 5 seconds to travel a mile, and it carries only about 10 miles. So if you can hear thunder, you're likely within striking distance. No place outside is safe then: when thunder roars, go indoors.

mascot.line: This is Level 5's rule in a new place: chill a melt fast enough and you get glass, not crystals.

cards.fact: Lightning that strikes sand can leave a tube of glass behind.
cards.context: It's called a fulgurite. The strike fuses silica (quartz) sand, and the melt cools and solidifies so fast that the inside of the tube turns glassy. Fulgurites turn up in clean, dry sand on beaches and in deserts.

title: How Hail Grows
objective: After this level you can explain how strong updrafts keep hailstones aloft long enough to grow layer by layer.
summary: Hailstones grow as updrafts lift them through supercooled water that freezes on contact, and fall when the updraft can no longer hold them. Milky layers froze fast, clear ones slowly.

cards.headline: Slice a big hailstone in half and you find rings, some milky, some clear.
cards.body: Like a tree's rings, they're a record. Each one tells you something about the stone's trip through the storm.

cards.headline: Born in the updraft
cards.body: Hail starts when a thunderstorm's updraft carries raindrops up into extremely cold parts of the cloud. Up there, water can stay liquid well below freezing. This supercooled water freezes the moment it touches ice, so a hailstone grows by colliding with it. A strong updraft keeps lifting the stone toward the top of the cloud, into more supercooled water. The stronger the updraft, the bigger the hailstone can grow.

cards.headline: Too heavy to hold
cards.body: Hail falls when the updraft can no longer support the weight of the ice, or when the updraft weakens. Here's a twist: Florida has the most thunderstorms in the US, yet the most hailstorms usually hit where Nebraska, Colorado and Wyoming meet. Over those high plains, the freezing level sits much closer to the ground, so hail has less time to melt on the way down.

cards.headline: Reading the rings
cards.body: Where the air is well below freezing and droplets are scarce, each droplet freezes the instant it hits, trapping tiny air bubbles: a milky layer. That's dry growth. Where it's just below freezing and water is plentiful, water spreads over the stone and freezes slowly, so the bubbles escape: a clear layer. That's wet growth. Counting the layers hints at how many times the stone traveled through the storm.

title: Supercells: Storms That Rotate
objective: After this level you can explain how changing winds with height set a supercell spinning and why it spawns the strongest tornadoes.
summary: Wind shear sets air rolling sideways; a strong updraft tips that spin upright into a rotating updraft, a mesocyclone. Supercells last hours and make the biggest hail and nearly all violent tornadoes.

cards.headline: The biggest hailstone ever measured in the US fell from one rotating storm.
cards.body: On July 23, 2010, a supercell over Vivian, South Dakota, dropped a stone of ice 8 inches across, weighing almost 2 pounds. What makes these storms so powerful?

cards.headline: Wind that changes with height
cards.body: A supercell needs wind shear: winds that change speed or direction as you go up. Picture the wind near the ground blowing from the southeast, while the wind higher up blows from the southwest, and faster. That difference sets the air in between rolling sideways, like a football spinning on its side.

cards.headline: Tipping the spin upright
cards.body: When a strong updraft draws in that rolling air, the updraft itself starts to rotate. A deep, persistent rotating updraft is called a mesocyclone, and it's what makes a supercell a supercell. The shear also tilts the storm, keeping its updraft apart from its downdraft. So the storm doesn't choke on its own rain the way Level 61's ordinary cell did, and it can last for several hours.

cards.fact: Virtually all of the most violent tornadoes come from supercells.
cards.context: So do the vast majority of significant ones. Even so, scientists are still studying exactly how a tornado forms inside one.

title: Tornado Alley and the EF Scale
objective: After this level you can explain why the central US gets so many tornadoes and how damage is used to rate them.
summary: Flat, fast-heating land, Gulf moisture and cooler northern air make the central US a tornado hotspot. The EF scale rates tornadoes afterward from their damage, so its winds are estimates.

cards.headline: The US averages about 1,200 tornadoes a year.
cards.body: Why do so many form in the middle of the country? And how do experts rate a tornado when nobody could measure its winds?

cards.headline: Why the middle of the country
cards.body: The central US is a big, fairly flat core, and the Great Plains and Mississippi River valley heat up quickly much of the year. Moisture flows in from the Gulf of Mexico, along with water vapor from the region's own plants, while cooler air arrives from the Upper Great Plains and Canada. Together they feed frequent outbreaks of severe thunderstorms. Forecasters stress that this recipe is a simplification: most storms in these setups never make a tornado, and nobody fully understands why some do.

cards.headline: Rated by what's left behind
cards.body: Nobody knows the true ground-level winds in most tornadoes. So since February 1, 2007, the US has rated them with the Enhanced Fujita (EF) scale. After a tornado, National Weather Service surveyors compare the damage with 28 damage indicators, from barns to schools, each with up to 8 degrees of damage. The rating reflects the strongest wind along the damage path. Its winds are estimates, not measurements.

mascot.line: Don't memorize the wind speeds. Remember the method: the EF scale reads the damage, then estimates the wind.

cards.fact: An EF5 tornado has estimated gusts of over 200 mph.
cards.context: The scale starts at EF0, with gusts of 65 to 85 mph. But a rating can only be as high as the damage surveyors can find. In 1999, part of an Oklahoma tornado that did top-level damage elsewhere was rated only F2 to F3 across a sparsely built valley, possibly because there was little there to wreck.

title: Inside a Hurricane
objective: After this level you can explain how the eye, the eyewall and the rain bands work together in a mature hurricane.
summary: A mature hurricane has a calm eye with the lowest pressure, a surrounding eyewall of towering thunderstorms with the strongest winds and heaviest rain, and long spiral rain bands farther out.

cards.headline: The calmest place in a hurricane is its very center.
cards.body: You met hurricanes in World Geography: storms that run on warm, moist air from the sea. A mature one is laid out like a target, with three very different zones.

cards.headline: The eye
cards.body: At the center sits the eye, a roughly circular area of fair weather. It's where the pressure at the surface is lowest. Eyes range from 5 to 120 miles across, but most are 20 to 40 miles. The air inside sinks slowly. Exactly how the eye forms is still debated by scientists.

cards.headline: The eyewall
cards.body: Around the eye stands the eyewall, a ring of towering thunderstorms. Warm, moist air rises here, cools, and its vapor condenses into droplets, building the tall clouds. The eyewall has the storm's highest surface winds, and more rain falls around it than in the outer bands. Oddly, it makes little lightning: its updrafts are too weak to carry much supercooled water, the charging ingredient from Level 62.

cards.headline: The rain bands
cards.body: Farther out, long, narrow bands of rain and thunderstorms spiral in toward the center, lined up with the wind. In some storms, a gap of lighter rain called the moat separates the eyewall from an outer band. Lightning is more common out in these bands than in the eyewall.

title: Why Category Isn't Everything
objective: After this level you can explain what the Saffir-Simpson scale measures and why water, not wind, causes most hurricane deaths.
summary: A hurricane's category rates only its sustained wind. Water causes most US hurricane deaths, and rain depends on a storm's speed and size, not its category.

cards.headline: A hurricane's category is about wind. The deadliest danger isn't in it.
cards.body: The 1 to 5 number is the first thing you hear about a hurricane. It's useful, but it leaves out the biggest danger of all.

mascot.line: People mix this up all the time: the category rates wind only. It says nothing about rain or storm surge.

cards.headline: What the number measures
cards.body: The Saffir-Simpson Hurricane Wind Scale rates a hurricane from 1 to 5 based only on its maximum sustained wind, and estimates the property damage that wind could do. Category 1 runs from 74 to 95 mph; Category 5 means 157 mph or more. Category 3 and up count as major hurricanes. What it leaves out: storm surge, flooding from rain and tornadoes. Hurricanes of every category can bring all three.

cards.fact: From 1963 to 2024, water caused about 80 percent of direct US deaths from hurricanes and tropical storms.
cards.context: Flooding from rain was the single biggest cause, just ahead of storm surge, the sea pushed ashore (The Oceans covers that one). Wind and tornadoes together caused far fewer deaths.

cards.headline: Slow and wide means wet
cards.body: How much rain a storm drops isn't tied to its strength. It depends on the storm's speed and size, and on the land below: slower, larger storms produce more rain, and mountains wring out even more. That's why flooding is the major threat for people living inland, far from any surge. Hurricanes of every category can bring deadly floods.

title: Nor'easters and Blizzards
objective: After this level you can explain how winter storms form along the US East Coast and what turns a snowstorm into a blizzard.
summary: Nor'easters are East Coast storms fed by the clash between cold continental air and air warmed over the Atlantic. A blizzard is defined by wind, visibility and time, not by how much snow falls.

cards.headline: A blizzard doesn't need any snow to be falling.
cards.body: Wind whipping up snow that's already on the ground can be enough. First, meet the East Coast storm that can bring heavy snow and fierce wind to big cities.

cards.headline: Named for the wind
cards.body: A nor'easter is a storm along the East Coast of North America, named because the winds over the coast typically blow from the northeast. They can come any time of year but are most frequent and most violent from September to April. Most form within 100 miles of the coast between Georgia and New Jersey, then strengthen as they head northeast toward New England.

cards.headline: Fueled by a temperature clash
cards.body: In winter, the jet stream carries cold Arctic air across Canada and the US toward the Atlantic. Offshore, the warm Gulf Stream keeps coastal waters relatively mild. The difference between cold air over land and warmer air over the water is the storm's fuel. The result is usually heavy rain or snow, gale-force winds and rough seas, and sometimes coastal flooding, especially along the busy corridor from Washington to Boston.

cards.headline: The blizzard checklist
cards.body: To the National Weather Service, a blizzard needs all of this at once: sustained winds or frequent gusts of 35 mph or more, and falling or blowing snow that often cuts visibility below a quarter mile, lasting 3 hours or longer. Notice what's missing: how much snow falls. When blowing snow alone does the job, it's called a ground blizzard.

title: Lake-Effect Snow
objective: After this level you can explain how cold air crossing warm lakes dumps narrow bands of very heavy snow.
summary: Cold air crossing the warmer, unfrozen Great Lakes picks up heat and moisture, rises and dumps narrow bands of heavy snow on downwind shores until the lakes freeze.

cards.headline: Sunshine here, and a mile away, 2 to 3 inches of snow an hour.
cards.body: Near the Great Lakes, that's an ordinary winter day. The lakes themselves make the snow.

cards.headline: Cold air, warm water
cards.body: It starts when cold air, often from Canada, crosses the open water of the Great Lakes in late fall and winter. The unfrozen lakes are warmer than that air, so they pass warmth and moisture into its lowest layer. Warmed from below, that air becomes lighter than the cold air above it, so it rises. Clouds form, and the lake's water comes down as snow on the downwind, or leeward, shores.

cards.headline: Narrow bands
cards.body: Lake-effect snow usually falls in narrow bands of intense snow. Sunny skies can turn to blinding snow within minutes, and totals can range from a trace to several inches over a short distance. Wind direction decides who gets buried: even a small shift sends the band to a different town.

cards.headline: More lake, more snow
cards.body: The farther the wind travels across open water, the more water the air picks up, and a bigger temperature difference between lake and air adds more. Most of that moisture falls within about 25 miles of the lake, though it can reach 100 miles. The season usually slows around February, when the lakes freeze over and the air can no longer take their moisture.

cards.headline: Lake-effect snow: explained
learned: Warm lakes heat and moisten cold air
The air rises and snows downwind
Narrow bands, set by the wind
Frozen lakes shut it off

title: Checkpoint: Storms
objective: After this level you can explain how heat, moisture and spinning air build thunderstorms, tornadoes, hurricanes and winter storms.
summary: Every storm here runs on rising warm, moist air; shear, rotation and structure make the difference. A landfalling hurricane can even carry tornadoes, which its wind-only category can't show.

cards.headline: Chapter 7 finale: one storm can hide the others inside it.
cards.body: A landfalling hurricane can carry thunderstorms, lightning, flooding rain and even tornadoes. First, the engine they all share.

cards.headline: Same engine, different shapes
cards.body: Every storm in this chapter runs on warm, moist air rising: its moisture condenses into cloud, and the storm grows. Inside, colliding ice charges it for lightning, and supercooled water builds hail layer by layer. The setup decides the rest. In an ordinary cell, the downdraft soon cuts off the updraft. Add wind shear and the storm tilts and spins into a long-lived supercell. Ring thunderstorms into an eyewall around a calm eye and you have a hurricane.

mascot.line: This connects the whole chapter: learn the engine, and each storm is a variation on it.

cards.fact: Hurricanes often spawn tornadoes, but not always.
cards.context: Some landfalling hurricanes produce no known tornadoes, while others cause major outbreaks. Hurricane Andrew (1992) made none across South Florida but several across the Deep South after crossing the Gulf. One more hazard the wind-only category can't show you.

Why wind shear turns an ordinary storm into a rotating supercell that can spawn tornadoes.

title: Why the Hottest Days Come Late
objective: After this level you can explain why the warmest weeks arrive well after the longest day of the year (seasonal lag).
summary: The hottest weeks come well after the longest day because daytime heating outpaces nighttime cooling for weeks. Slow-warming water is the main reason, so the lag is longest near cool coasts.

cards.headline: The longest day is in June. The hottest days usually aren't.
cards.body: Across most of the contiguous US, the hottest day of the year comes, on average, between July 15 and 31. By then the days are already getting shorter. So why does the heat keep climbing?

cards.headline: Still filling the tank
cards.body: In the Northern Hemisphere, sunlight peaks at the summer solstice, around June 21. But temperature follows a running balance, not today's sunshine alone. For several weeks after the solstice, the sun's heating by day still beats the cooling by night, so the warmth keeps piling up. Think of a bathtub with the tap turned down a little: it keeps filling as long as more pours in than drains out.

mascot.line: People mix these up: the sunniest day isn't the hottest one. Heat piles up first, so the peak comes weeks later.

cards.headline: The same delay, on a bigger clock
cards.body: You already know a small version of this. The warmest part of the day usually comes several hours after noon, when the sun is highest. The seasons do the same thing, because ground and water take time to heat up. Winter lags too: in the UK, the coldest weather usually arrives in January or February, well after the December solstice.

cards.fact: Water covers over 70% of Earth's surface, and it warms far more slowly than land.
cards.context: Water has a much higher heat capacity: it takes more heat, and more time, to warm it up. That's the main reason for seasonal lag. Near chilly water the lag can stretch a long way. In San Francisco, a marine layer of low clouds over the cold coastal sea keeps early summer cool, and normal daily highs don't peak until October 2.

title: The Köppen Climate Map
objective: After this level you can explain how climates are classified by temperature and rainfall and read a place's climate type.
summary: Köppen's first letter sorts climates by temperature, except dry B. Later letters add rainfall and heat, so Cs, the Mediterranean climate, means mild with a dry summer.

cards.headline: Southern California and the Mediterranean coast share one climate code: Cs.
cards.body: Two letters, and a climate scientist can picture the summers and the winters. You met Köppen's five climate groups in World Geography. Now learn to read the code itself.

cards.headline: First letter: how warm?
cards.body: The first letter sorts by temperature, with one exception. A tropical climate (A) has no month cooler than 18 °C. A polar climate (E) has no month warmer than 10 °C. C and D are midlatitude climates in between, also set by temperature. The odd one out is B: dry climates are defined by dryness, not heat. So a desert can be scorching or freezing and still be a B.

cards.headline: Next letters: when does it rain?
cards.body: The second letter tracks rainfall through the year: f means no dry season, s means a dry summer, and w means a dry winter. In the B group it's different: W marks a true desert and S a semiarid steppe. A third letter can add heat: h for hot, k for cold. So BWh is a hot desert, and BWk is a cold one.

cards.headline: Reading Cs
cards.body: Put it together. C means a mild midlatitude climate, and s means the summer is the dry season. That's the Mediterranean climate: hot, dry summers and cool, wet winters. It sits between about 30° and 45° latitude on the western sides of continents, which is how southern California ends up sharing a code with the Mediterranean coast.
cards.callout: A, C, D, E: temperature · B: dryness · f / s / w: when the dry season falls

title: The Fast Carbon Cycle
objective: After this level you can explain how carbon moves each year between the air, plants, soil and ocean.
summary: Plants and phytoplankton pull carbon dioxide from the air to build sugar. Respiration, decay and fire send it back within a lifespan, and soil's decaying matter is part of that loop.

cards.headline: Every leaf is borrowed carbon, and the loan comes due within a lifetime.
cards.body: Carbon shuttles between the air and living things on the timescale of a lifespan. That's the fast carbon cycle: fast by Earth's standards, if not by yours.

cards.headline: Carbon in: building with air
cards.body: Plants on land and phytoplankton in the sea are the main players. Using energy from sunlight, they combine carbon dioxide from the air with water to make sugar, and they release oxygen. (Chemistry covers how photosynthesis works.) That sugar becomes leaves, wood and roots. A growing forest is carbon pulled out of the sky.

cards.headline: Carbon out: four ways home
cards.body: The carbon doesn't stay put. Plants break down some of their sugar for energy. Animals, you included, eat plants or plankton and do the same. When plants and plankton die, bacteria eat them and they decay. And sometimes fire burns them. All four routes usually end the same way: carbon dioxide back in the air.

cards.headline: The soil's slow exhale
cards.body: Remember Level 9's soil? About 5% of a healthy soil is organic matter: the decaying remains of once-living things. That's the fast cycle's waiting room. Dead plants keep refilling it, and bacteria keep emptying it, breathing the carbon back out as carbon dioxide.

learned: Plants and phytoplankton pull carbon from the air

title: Earth's Slow Thermostat
objective: After this level you can explain how rock weathering and volcanoes balance carbon dioxide over millions of years.
summary: Carbonic acid rain dissolves rock, and the dissolved minerals become limestone in the sea. Volcanoes return the carbon, and because weathering speeds up when it's warm, the cycle acts as a thermostat.

cards.headline: Most of Earth's carbon isn't in the air or in living things. It's in rock.
cards.body: The rest is spread through the ocean, the air, plants, soil and fossil fuels. And that rock is part of a slow thermostat, run by rain, shells and volcanoes.

cards.headline: Rain that dissolves rock
cards.body: Carbon dioxide from the air mixes with rainwater to make a weak acid, carbonic acid. When that rain lands on rock, it slowly dissolves it. That's chemical weathering. The carbon doesn't vanish: it washes along with the dissolved minerals to the ocean.

cards.headline: Shells into stone
cards.body: In the sea, shell builders such as corals and plankton use the calcium from weathered rock to make calcium carbonate. When they die, their shells settle, and the layers are cemented into limestone, Level 6's rock of ancient shells. Carbon that once fell as rain is now locked away for millions of years.

mascot.line: Keep this: weathering speeds up when it's warm and slows when it's cold. That's what makes it a thermostat.

cards.headline: Volcanoes close the loop
cards.body: Rock doesn't keep its carbon forever. Carbon-bearing rock carried deep into the Earth melts, and volcanoes vent the carbon as carbon dioxide. Here's the thermostat: if volcanoes push carbon dioxide up, the planet warms, and warmth brings more rain and faster weathering. That sends more carbon to the ocean floor, and the warming eases.

title: Snowball Earth and Hothouse Earth
objective: After this level you can describe Earth's most extreme past climates and what the rocks tell us about them.
summary: Rocks suggest ice once reached the Equator, until volcanic carbon dioxide thawed the planet and left cap carbonates behind. At the other extreme, ice-free poles grew Arctic palms.

cards.headline: Earth has frozen near the Equator, and grown palm trees in the Arctic.
cards.body: Both extremes left clues in the rocks. Read them, and the same control knob keeps showing up.

cards.headline: Snowball Earth
cards.body: The Cryogenian Period, about 720 to 635 million years ago, takes its name from the Greek for frost or ice, and for good reason: much if not all of Earth froze. The key clue is ice-laid deposits that, magnetic evidence shows, formed near the Equator. If ice reached the tropics, the Snowball Earth hypothesis says, it reached from pole to pole. Some scientists argue for a 'Slushball' with open water; the debate isn't settled.

cards.headline: How to thaw a snowball
cards.body: Volcanoes never stopped venting carbon dioxide. Weathering and photosynthesis, which normally pull it back out, were suppressed on a frozen planet. So the gas built up until its greenhouse warming melted the ice. The rocks record the flip: layered limestone or dolomite, called cap carbonates, sits directly on the glacial deposits at over 50 places, from Death Valley to Namibia.

cards.headline: Hothouse Earth
cards.body: Now the other extreme. About 56 million years ago, the poles had no ice caps, and palm trees grew above the Arctic Circle. A 2024 study that rebuilt 485 million years of global temperature summed up the pattern. In paleoclimatologist Jessica Tierney's words: 'carbon dioxide is the dominant control on global temperatures across geological time.'

title: Reading Ice Cores
objective: After this level you can explain how air bubbles in ancient ice record 800,000 years of carbon dioxide and temperature.
summary: Buried snow is squeezed into ice that seals in bubbles of old air. The bubbles record carbon dioxide and the ice records temperature, back 800,000 years.

cards.headline: Antarctic ice holds bubbles of air from 800,000 years ago.
cards.body: Drill down about 3 km and you're reading the planet's diary, one snowfall at a time.

cards.headline: Snow into a time capsule
cards.body: Each year's snow buries the last. Pressed by the weight above, snow turns into denser firn and then solid ice, and air gets sealed into tiny bubbles on the way. Those bubbles are real samples of the old atmosphere. Seasons leave yearly layers in the ice too, like tree rings, though they get harder to see deeper down.

cards.headline: Two records in one core
cards.body: One core holds two diaries. The bubbles give the gases directly: scientists extract the air and measure its carbon dioxide and methane. The ice itself gives the temperature, through the ratios of different isotopes, slightly different forms, of the water it's made of.

cards.fact: Over 800,000 years, carbon dioxide and temperature rose and fell together.
cards.context: The EPICA Dome C core from Antarctica shows long, cold glacial periods broken roughly every 100,000 years by warm interglacials. We're in one now: the last 11,000 years. Carbon dioxide ran low in the cold times and high in the warm ones. What sets that slow beat is Level 77's story.

title: Earth's Wobbles and the Ice Ages
objective: After this level you can explain how slow changes in Earth's orbit and tilt (Milankovitch cycles) pace the ice ages.
summary: Slow cycles in Earth's orbit shape, tilt and wobble decide how warm northern summers are. When they're cool, snow survives and ice sheets grow, as seafloor shells confirmed in 1976.

cards.headline: Earth wobbles like a spinning top, and the ice ages keep time with it.
cards.body: Level 76's ice core showed a slow beat of cold and warm. The metronome turns out to be Earth's own orbit.

items.label: Eccentricity
points: The shape of Earth's orbit
About 100,000 years

items.label: Obliquity
points: The tilt of the axis, 22.1° to 24.5°
About 41,000 years

items.label: Precession
points: A wobble of the axis, like a top
About 26,000 years

mascot.line: Keep this: ice sheets grow when northern summers are too cool to melt the winter's snow.

cards.headline: It's all about summer
cards.body: Serbian scientist Milutin Milankovitch, born in 1879, asked which season matters most. His answer: summer in the far north. When those summers run cool, less of the winter's snow melts, and it piles up year after year into ice sheets. Growing ice then reflects more sunlight back to space, cooling things further, so a small nudge can grow.

cards.headline: Proof from the seafloor
cards.body: In 1976 a study titled 'Pacemaker of the Ice Ages' read deep-sea sediment cores covering 450,000 years, and the big climate swings matched the orbital cycles. A key clue: oxygen isotopes in the shells of foraminifera, single-celled sea creatures whose shells pile up into limestone and chalk. Ice ages once came about every 41,000 years; about 800,000 years ago the beat stretched to 100,000, and scientists still aren't sure why.

title: The World of the Last Ice Age
objective: After this level you can describe what the planet looked like about 20,000 years ago, when ice sheets covered much of North America.
summary: Twenty thousand years ago Earth was about 6 °C colder, with ice over North America to Wisconsin. The world was dry and dusty, and grinding ice left loess that now makes fertile soil.

cards.headline: At the peak of the last ice age, Earth was only about 6 °C colder than today.
cards.body: That was enough to push ice sheets as far south as Wisconsin. As paleoclimatologist Jessica Tierney put it, that is 'a huge change.'

cards.headline: A frozen north
cards.body: About 20,000 years ago, at the Last Glacial Maximum, Earth's average temperature was about 8 °C. You met the lower seas and the Bering land bridge in World Geography. Here's more of the picture: the Laurentide, Cordilleran and Greenland ice sheets spread across North America, reaching as far south as Wisconsin.

cards.headline: Dry, dusty and low on carbon
cards.body: An ice-age world wasn't just colder; it was drier. Less moisture meant fewer plants and bigger deserts, and dust filled the air. Carbon dioxide sank as low as about 180 parts per million.

cards.headline: Ice-age dust you can farm
cards.body: Grinding ice sheets crushed rock into fine powder, and winds carried the silt far away as loess. Loess now covers about 10% of Earth's land, including plains along the Mississippi and Missouri valleys. It carries quartz and feldspar, Chapter 1's old friends, and the soils that form on it are typically fertile and good for intensive farming.

title: When Volcanoes Cool the World
objective: After this level you can explain how big eruptions like Tambora and Pinatubo cooled the globe for a year or two.
summary: Big eruptions cool the planet through sulfur lofted into the stratosphere, not ash. Tambora brought 1816's 'year without a summer', and Pinatubo cooled Earth about 0.5 °C in 1992.

cards.headline: In 1816, frost and snow struck Europe and North America in midsummer.
cards.body: People called it the 'year without a summer.' The cause was a volcano on the far side of the world that had erupted the year before.

cards.headline: Tambora's long reach
cards.body: Mount Tambora in Indonesia erupted in April 1815, the largest volcanic event in recorded history. You saw the trick in Level 1: the ash soon falls out, but sulfur dioxide in the stratosphere becomes droplets of sulfuric acid that reflect sunlight. In 1816, western Europe and eastern North America saw heavy snow and killing frost through June, July and August, and crops failed.

cards.headline: Pinatubo, measured
cards.body: In June 1991, Mount Pinatubo in the Philippines put a haze of sulfate droplets into the stratosphere. Within about 3 weeks it had circled the globe, and within about a year it covered it. Instruments caught the result: an estimated 0.5 °C of global cooling in 1992. Like the other big eruptions of the past century, it was a dent that lasted one to three years, not a new climate.

cards.fact: A bigger eruption isn't always a colder one.
cards.context: The volume of magma a volcano erupts and the amount of sulfur dioxide it releases don't always go together. What matters for climate is the sulfur that reaches the stratosphere and turns into sunlight-reflecting droplets. The ash, however dramatic, falls out within days to weeks.

learned: Tambora's eruption brought 1816's cold summer

title: Checkpoint: Climates Past and Present
objective: After this level you can explain how sunlight, orbit, carbon and volcanoes have set Earth's climate from the ice ages to today.
summary: Orbital cycles pace the ice ages while carbon dioxide and ice amplify them. Across the chapter, carbon dioxide sets the long-term dial; volcanoes and seasons only nudge it for a while.

cards.headline: Chapter 8 finale: Earth's climate has dials that turn on very different clocks.
cards.body: A summer peaks several weeks late. A big eruption chills the world for one to three years. Orbital cycles swing over tens of thousands of years, and rock locks carbon away for millions. Here's how the dials fit together.

mascot.line: This is Levels 76 and 77 working together: the orbit sets the beat, and carbon and ice turn up the volume.

cards.headline: Pacemaker and amplifier
cards.body: Level 77's orbital cycles set the timing of the ice ages, but on their own they cause only small changes. Carbon dioxide and ice amplify them: as ice retreats, less sunlight is reflected, and rising carbon dioxide adds more warming. In Antarctic ice, temperature and carbon dioxide climbed together through most of the roughly 6,000-year warming out of the last ice age.

cards.headline: The same knob, every time
cards.body: Look back and carbon dioxide keeps turning up. It built up when volcanoes outran weathering and thawed Snowball Earth. It gets locked into limestone for millions of years. It rose and fell with the ice ages in Antarctic bubbles. Across 485 million years, it has been the dominant control on global temperature. A volcano's sulfur can chill the world for one to three years; carbon sets the long-term dial.

title: The Keeling Curve
objective: After this level you can read the record of carbon dioxide since 1958 and explain both its steady rise and its yearly zigzag.
summary: Carbon dioxide measured at Mauna Loa since 1958 climbs every year because sinks absorb only half our emissions, and it zigzags as northern plants grow and decay.

cards.headline: Each May, Hawaii's air holds more carbon dioxide than in any other month.
cards.body: One graph from a Hawaiian volcano shows two things at once: a line that climbs every single year, and a wobble that repeats every single year. Learn to read both.

cards.headline: A flask of air on a volcano
cards.body: In March 1958, C. David Keeling of the Scripps Institution of Oceanography began measuring carbon dioxide at Mauna Loa Observatory in Hawaii. The record never stopped, and it is now the longest direct record of CO2 in the air. The Keeling Curve started at about 315 parts per million (ppm). In 2024 the yearly average at Mauna Loa was about 425 ppm. Before the Industrial Revolution, it was 280 ppm or less.

cards.headline: Why the line only climbs
cards.body: Each year people release carbon dioxide by burning fossil fuels. Plant growth and the ocean soak up about half of it. The other half stays in the air, so the total ratchets up year after year. That is how the air came to hold about 50 percent more CO2 than before the Industrial Revolution. Think of a bathtub with the tap running faster than the drain.

cards.headline: The yearly zigzag
cards.body: Zoom in and the line wiggles like a saw blade. In Northern Hemisphere spring and summer, plants draw carbon dioxide in to grow, and the level falls. In autumn and winter, growth slows and dead leaves decay, releasing it again. At Mauna Loa the peak comes each May. The Southern Hemisphere does the same in opposite seasons, only weaker, because the north has far more land and plants. You are watching the planet breathe.

title: How We Know the Extra Carbon Is Ours
objective: After this level you can explain the chemical fingerprints that trace the rise in carbon dioxide to fossil fuels.
summary: Fossil carbon is low in carbon-13 and has no carbon-14, and the air's isotopes are shifting to match; falling oxygen and tiny volcanic emissions point the same way.

cards.headline: Tailpipe and volcano carbon dioxide look the same. Their atoms don't.
cards.body: The air has gained carbon dioxide, but could it have come from somewhere other than us? Scientists checked the carbon atoms themselves, like detectives checking fingerprints.

cards.headline: Plants leave a light fingerprint
cards.body: Carbon comes in slightly different weights. Plants hold less of the heavier carbon-13 than the air does. Coal and oil are the remains of ancient plants and animals, so they carry that same low-carbon-13 fingerprint. And as we burn them, the share of carbon-13 in the air is steadily falling. The extra carbon looks exactly like old plant carbon.

cards.headline: Too old to carry carbon-14
cards.body: Fossil fuels also contain no carbon-14, the heaviest form of carbon (Chemistry explains why it fades). Measurements of carbon-14 in the air show that the rise in carbon dioxide is dominated by fossil fuel emissions. Coal and oil hold carbon that plants pulled from the air over millions of years of photosynthesis. We are returning it in a few hundred.

mascot.line: Keep this: carbon-13, carbon-14 and oxygen are three separate clues, and all three point to fossil fuels.

cards.headline: Two more clues
cards.body: Burning fuel uses up oxygen, and the air's oxygen is slowly falling worldwide, mainly because of fossil fuel burning (far too little to affect your breathing). And volcanoes? Human activities emit 60 or more times as much carbon dioxide each year as all the world's volcanoes. Every clue points the same way.

title: Measuring a Warming World
objective: After this level you can explain how scientists build the global temperature record and what it shows since the 1800s.
summary: The record joins land stations with ship, buoy and satellite sea readings as anomalies; independent groups agree Earth was about 1.1 °C warmer in 2011 to 2020 than in 1850 to 1900.

cards.headline: An average temperature for a whole planet sounds impossible.
cards.body: Right now one place is baking while another freezes. So how can anyone spot a warming of about a degree across the whole Earth? The trick is to stop comparing places with each other and compare each place with itself.

cards.headline: Thermometers on land and sea
cards.body: Weather stations measure the air on land, but land covers only about a third of the planet. For the rest, the record uses sea surface temperatures from ships and buoys, and more recently from satellites. Stitch the two together and you get a global record that reaches back to the 1800s.

cards.headline: Compare each place with itself
cards.body: Instead of averaging raw temperatures, scientists turn each reading into an anomaly: how much warmer or colder it was than the long-term average for that place and date. A desert and a mountaintop can't be averaged sensibly, but their changes can. Several independent research groups run the numbers their own way, and they all find a similar upward trend.

cards.fact: Earth's surface was about 1.1 °C warmer in 2011 to 2020 than in 1850 to 1900.
cards.context: That is the IPCC's figure, and land warmed more than the ocean. Each of the last four decades has also been warmer than every decade before it since 1850. One hot year could be luck. Four decades climbing like stairs is a trend.

title: Ruling Out the Sun and Volcanoes
objective: After this level you can weigh natural causes against greenhouse gases as explanations for recent warming.
summary: The Sun's output shows no upward trend since 1978 and the stratosphere is cooling; volcanoes cool Earth only briefly. The IPCC finds natural drivers added about zero warming.

cards.headline: The Sun heats our planet. So why isn't it behind the recent warming?
cards.body: It's a fair suspect, and so are volcanoes. A good detective checks every alibi before naming a culprit. Here are the two natural suspects, and the evidence that clears them.

cards.headline: Suspect one: the Sun
cards.body: Since 1978, sensors on satellites have measured how much of the Sun's energy reaches the top of our atmosphere. They show no upward trend. Earth warmed anyway. You can't blame a rising temperature on a heater whose dial hasn't moved.

cards.headline: The giveaway in the sky
cards.body: There's a second clue. A brighter Sun would warm every layer of the atmosphere, from the ground up through the stratosphere. Instead, the surface is warming while the stratosphere is cooling. That is the pattern you expect when gases trap heat down low, not when the Sun turns up.

cards.headline: Suspect two: volcanoes
cards.body: Level 1 showed that a big eruption cools the planet for one to three years before the effect fades. That makes a dip, not a long climb. Add up every natural driver, the Sun and volcanoes together, and the IPCC finds they changed global temperature by only -0.1 to +0.1 °C between 1850 to 1900 and 2010 to 2019. Human causes likely account for 0.8 to 1.3 °C.

title: Feedbacks: Melting Ice and Water Vapor
objective: After this level you can explain how melting ice and extra water vapor amplify an initial warming.
summary: Feedbacks amplify or damp a change. Melting snow exposes darker ground that absorbs more sunlight, and warmer air holds more water vapor, which traps more heat.

cards.headline: Warm the planet a little, and it finds ways to warm itself a bit more.
cards.body: Scientists call these loops feedbacks. Two of the strongest involve things you already know well: bright white snow and invisible water vapor.

cards.headline: Loops that amplify
cards.body: A feedback is a loop in which a change sets off effects that feed back on it. A positive feedback amplifies the change; a negative feedback reduces it. Positive doesn't mean good here. It means more of the same, like a microphone squealing when it picks up its own speaker.

cards.headline: White snow, dark ground
cards.body: Snow reflects 80 to 90 percent of sunlight. Trees, plants and soil reflect only 10 to 30 percent. So when warming melts snow, darker ground takes its place and soaks up more sunlight, which warms things further and melts more snow. It's the reason black clothes feel hotter in the sun than white ones, scaled up to a planet.

mascot.line: Common mix-up: water vapor is the most abundant greenhouse gas, but it amplifies warming. It doesn't start it.

cards.headline: The vapor amplifier
cards.body: For every 1 °C of warming, the air can hold about 7 percent more water vapor. Vapor is a greenhouse gas, so the extra traps more heat, which allows still more vapor. Scientists estimate this loop more than doubles the warming from carbon dioxide alone. Yet vapor isn't the driver: a molecule stays aloft only about nine days before it rains out, so it follows the temperature rather than setting it.

title: Climate Sensitivity
objective: After this level you can explain how much warming scientists expect from doubling carbon dioxide and why the range is uncertain.
summary: Doubling CO2 would eventually warm Earth by about 3 °C, likely 2.5 to 4 °C (IPCC AR6). Clouds are the main reason the answer is still a range.

cards.headline: Double the carbon dioxide in the air. How much warmer does Earth end up?
cards.body: It may be the most important question in climate science, and the answer isn't a single number. It's a range, and the story is why.

cards.headline: One question, one name
cards.body: Scientists call it equilibrium climate sensitivity: the warming Earth eventually settles at after the carbon dioxide in the air doubles and the climate adjusts. Level 81 gave the starting point: 280 ppm or less before the Industrial Revolution. The answer counts everything that responds along the way, including the snow and water vapor feedbacks from Level 85.

cards.fact: IPCC's best estimate: doubling carbon dioxide eventually warms Earth about 3 °C, likely 2.5 to 4 °C.
cards.context: In IPCC language, likely means a 66 to 100% chance. The very likely range is 2 to 5 °C. The 2021 report narrowed the old likely range of 1.5 to 4.5 °C by combining several lines of evidence: how climate works, the measured record, past climates and models.

cards.headline: Why clouds keep it a range
cards.body: The biggest remaining uncertainty is clouds: how their amount and type will shift as the world warms. That's why sensitivity is still a range rather than one number. But the IPCC now judges it very unlikely that clouds will turn out to damp the warming, and its very likely range starts at 2 °C, not near zero.

title: Ice Sheets in Retreat
objective: After this level you can explain how Greenland and Antarctica are losing ice and why their slow response matters for centuries.
summary: Satellites show Greenland and Antarctica losing ice since 2002 through surface melt and outlet glaciers. Both are committed to losses for decades or centuries.

cards.headline: Satellites can weigh an ice sheet from space.
cards.body: Since 2002, the GRACE satellites, short for Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment, have tracked the ice on Greenland and Antarctica. Both scales read in the same direction.

cards.headline: Two giants losing weight
cards.body: Earth's two ice sheets cap Greenland and Antarctica. Since 2002, Greenland has lost roughly 260 billion tons of ice a year and Antarctica roughly 135 billion. That's ice you could never see go from a beach chair, but the satellites keep the books.

cards.headline: Melting from above and at the edges
cards.body: The ice goes in two main ways. In Greenland, the surface melts in summer, and the IPCC finds human influence has very likely contributed to that melting over the past two decades. At the edges of both sheets, large outlet glaciers carry ice to the sea, and warming ocean water near them plays a key role in the losses. For Antarctica, evidence of the human part is still limited.

cards.headline: A slow, long commitment
cards.body: Ice sheets respond slowly, and they keep responding. The IPCC says glaciers are committed to keep melting for decades or centuries: continued ice loss this century is virtually certain for Greenland and likely for Antarctica. The pace is the open question. Rare instabilities, some involving tipping points, could sharply speed Antarctic losses under high emissions, but their odds carry deep uncertainty.

objective: After this level you can name the main human sources of greenhouse gases, from power and transport to farming and forests.
summary: In 2019, energy supply made about 34% of human greenhouse gas emissions, then industry, land use, transport and buildings. Cement even releases CO2 from limestone itself.

cards.headline: More than a fifth of greenhouse gas emissions come from farms, forests and land.
cards.body: Power plants and cars get the headlines, but the full list is longer and more surprising. Here is where the gases come from, sector by sector and gas by gas.

cards.headline: Five sectors
cards.body: The IPCC split 2019's human greenhouse gas emissions into five sectors. Energy supply came first at about 34%. Industry made 24%, agriculture, forestry and other land use 22%, transport 15% and buildings 6%. Burning coal, natural gas and oil for electricity and heat is the largest single source.

cards.headline: Not just carbon dioxide
cards.body: Carbon dioxide comes mainly from burning fossil fuels, but also from cutting down forests and clearing land. Methane comes from agriculture, waste, energy production and burning plants. Nitrous oxide comes mainly from agriculture, such as fertilizer use. So a cleared forest and a fertilized field both belong on the list, not just a tailpipe.

cards.headline: Carbon from the rock itself
cards.body: Cement has a twist. To make it, limestone is heated until its calcium carbonate breaks down into lime and carbon dioxide, so the gas comes straight out of the rock. The fuel burned to heat the kilns adds more. Remember Level 6: much limestone is built from the shells of ancient sea creatures. Cement sends their long-stored carbon back into the air.

title: Extreme Weather and Attribution
objective: After this level you can explain how warming shifts the odds of heat waves and downpours and how scientists test a single event.
summary: Warming has made heatwaves and downpours more frequent and intense. Attribution studies compare today's climate with one without human influence; tornado links remain uncertain.

cards.headline: Scientists don't ask if warming caused a storm. They ask a sharper question.
cards.body: How much more likely, or how much stronger, did warming make it? That question has answers, and for some kinds of weather the answer is very clear.

cards.headline: Loaded dice
cards.body: The IPCC finds it virtually certain that heatwaves and other hot extremes have become more frequent and more intense over most land since the 1950s, with human-caused warming the main driver. Heavy downpours have increased too. Part of the reason is from Level 85: for every 1 °C of warming, the air can hold about 7 percent more water vapor, so storms have more water to drop.

cards.headline: Testing one event
cards.body: To test a single event, scientists run computer models twice: once for today's climate and once with the human influence removed. Comparing them shows how much more likely or intense the event became. For the record July 2019 heatwave in France and the Netherlands, World Weather Attribution found climate change made it at least 10 times more likely.

mascot.line: People mix this up: attribution doesn't say warming caused a storm. It measures how much warming loaded the dice.

cards.headline: Not every extreme is the same
cards.body: The evidence is strongest for heat and heavy rain. For tornadoes, scientists have low confidence in any link to climate change so far: tornadoes are small and short-lived, which makes them very hard to model. Good science says "we know" where it knows, and "not yet" where it doesn't.
