title: How a Forecast Is Made
objective: After this level you can explain how weather balloons, radar, satellites and computer models turn observations into a forecast.
summary: A forecast starts with a snapshot of the atmosphere from weather balloons, Doppler radar and satellites; a computer model then solves the physics step by step into the future.

cards.headline: Twice a day, weather balloons rise at the same moment all over the world.
cards.body: Every forecast begins with a snapshot of the whole atmosphere, taken at once. Balloons, radar and satellites take the picture. A computer turns it into tomorrow.

cards.headline: The balloon that phones home
cards.body: Hanging under each balloon is a radiosonde, a small box of instruments. Every second it radios back the air pressure, temperature and humidity, plus its GPS position; tracking that position gives the wind. It can climb past 35 km, drawing a thin line of readings up through the sky. The National Weather Service launches from 92 stations, in step with hundreds more around the world.

cards.fact: A weather radar transmits for only about 7 seconds an hour. The rest of the time, it listens.
cards.context: Each pulse scatters off raindrops, snow, hail, even bugs, and a sliver bounces back. The echo's strength and travel time show what's out there and how far away. Its Doppler shift, the effect that changes a passing train whistle's pitch, shows whether the target is moving toward or away from the radar.

cards.headline: A satellite that never looks away
cards.body: GOES weather satellites orbit 22,236 miles above the Equator, moving exactly as fast as Earth turns. So each one hangs over the same region and watches it without a break. Balloons give you thin lines through the air; the satellite gives you the whole scene from above, all day and all night.

cards.headline: The model does the math
cards.body: Now a computer takes over. A weather model pulls in observations from satellites, aircraft, balloons and even backyard weather stations to build a picture of the atmosphere right now. Then it solves the equations of physics for temperature, dew point, wind and more, at the ground and at many layers above. It takes one small step forward in time, feeds the answer back in and repeats, over and over, until it reaches days ahead.

learned: Balloons sample the air every second
Doppler radar finds rain and its motion
Satellites watch one region nonstop

title: What a 40% Chance of Rain Means
objective: After this level you can interpret a probability forecast and explain why forecasts lose skill after about a week or two.
summary: A 40% chance of rain is the odds of measurable rain at your spot. Skill fades because small errors grow in a chaotic atmosphere; beyond two weeks, slow parts of Earth carry the signal.

cards.headline: A 40% chance of rain doesn't mean rain for 40% of the day.
cards.body: It doesn't mean rain over 40% of town, either. The real meaning is more useful, and it hides a deep fact about the atmosphere.

cards.headline: What the percentage means
cards.body: In a National Weather Service forecast, the chance of rain is the probability that at least 0.01 inch falls at your spot during the forecast period. So 40% means a 40% chance of measurable rain where you are. It isn't a share of the day or a share of the map. It's how likely.

cards.fact: A 5-day forecast is right about 90% of the time. A 10-day forecast, only about half.
cards.context: A 7-day forecast lands around 80%, says NOAA. The further out you go, the more the models have to lean on estimates and assumptions, so every extra day costs accuracy.

cards.headline: Why skill fades
cards.body: The atmosphere is chaotic. Observations are limited and unevenly spread, so the starting picture always holds small errors, and in a chaotic system small errors grow until they swamp the forecast. Forecasters fight back by running the model many times from slightly different starts. The spread of those runs becomes the probability in your forecast.

cards.headline: Beyond two weeks, ask the slow parts
cards.body: Day-by-day forecasts run out of road at around two weeks. For weeks to months ahead, forecasters turn to parts of Earth that change slowly and keep a memory of their state: heat stored in the upper ocean, sea ice, snowpack and soil moisture. The fast air forgets. The slow parts remember.

cards.headline: Forecast odds: decoded
learned: A rain chance is a probability for your spot
Skill fades as small errors grow
Many model runs become the odds
Slow parts of Earth help weeks ahead

title: Watches Versus Warnings
objective: After this level you can tell a watch from a warning and decide what to do for a tornado, a flood or a hurricane.
summary: A watch means conditions favor a hazard, so get ready; a warning means it's happening or about to, so act. Tornado warnings mean an interior room on the lowest floor, and volcanoes use the same words.

cards.headline: Watch and warning sound alike. One says get ready. The other says act now.
cards.body: Mixing them up costs the one thing you can't get back in a storm: time. Here's the difference, and what each one asks of you.

cards.headline: Watch: be prepared
cards.body: A watch means the ingredients are in place. A tornado watch says tornadoes are possible in and near a big area, often many counties or even several states. A flood watch says conditions favor flooding; it may not happen, but it could. Your job: review your plan, check your supplies and your safe room, and be ready to move fast.

mascot.line: People mix these up all the time. Watch: the ingredients are there. Warning: it's already cooking, so act now.

cards.headline: Warning: take action
cards.body: A warning means the danger is happening or about to. A tornado warning means a tornado has been sighted or picked up on radar, with imminent danger to life. It covers a much smaller area, about the size of a city or a small county. A flash flood warning means a flash flood is imminent or already under way.

points: Interior room, lowest floor, sturdy building
Stay away from windows
Mobile home, car or outdoors: get to the nearest sturdy shelter

items.label: Flash flood
points: In a flood-prone spot: move to high ground right away

items.label: Hurricane
points: Watch: about 48 hours before tropical-storm winds
Warning: about 36 hours before; finish preparing
Evacuate right away if ordered

cards.fact: Volcanoes get watches and warnings too.
cards.context: The USGS rates a volcano Normal, Advisory, Watch or Warning. Watch means unrest is building and an eruption is more likely. Warning means a hazardous eruption is imminent, underway or suspected. Same logic as the weather alerts.

title: Ready for an Earthquake
objective: After this level you can explain why quakes cannot be predicted and why Drop, Cover and Hold On is the advice.
summary: No one can predict an earthquake's date, place and size, so scientists give odds and people prepare. When the shaking starts: Drop, Cover and Hold On, because falling objects cause most injuries.

cards.headline: No scientist has ever predicted a major earthquake.
cards.body: Yet millions of people practice for them. That isn't a contradiction. It's the whole strategy.

cards.headline: Forecast, not predict
cards.body: A real prediction has to name three things: the date and time, the place and the size. Nobody, the USGS included, has ever done that for a major quake, and scientists don't expect to any time soon. What they can do is work out the odds: the probability of a significant quake in a given area within a certain number of years. You can't know when, so you get ready now.

cards.fact: There's no such thing as earthquake weather.
cards.context: Quakes strike about equally in heat, cold and rain. Most start several kilometers down, deeper than rainwater can easily reach. Hot, still afternoons have a reputation they don't deserve.

cards.headline: Drop, Cover and Hold On
cards.body: When the shaking starts, drop onto your hands and knees before it knocks you down. Cover your head and neck, crawling under a sturdy table or desk if one is close. Hold on until the shaking stops, ready to move with your shelter if it slides. In bed? Stay there, face down, with a pillow over your head and neck.

mascot.line: Common mix-up: the strongest-looking spot isn't the safest. The danger is what falls, so get under something sturdy.

cards.headline: Why not the doorway?
cards.body: Most quake injuries and deaths come from falling or flying things (TVs, lamps, glass, bookcases) or from being thrown to the floor. A doorway does nothing about a falling lamp. And running outside or to another room means moving while the floor moves: you're less likely to be hurt if you stay where you are.

cards.headline: Quake ready
learned: Quakes get odds, not predictions
There's no earthquake weather
Drop, Cover and Hold On

title: Heat: The Quiet Killer
objective: After this level you can explain why extreme heat is so dangerous, why cities run hotter, and who is most at risk.
summary: Extreme heat is the top weather killer in the US. Humid air slows cooling by sweat, heat stroke is a 911 emergency, and cities stay hotter, especially at night.

cards.headline: The deadliest weather in the US doesn't roar.
cards.body: No funnel, no thunder, no rushing water. The National Weather Service calls extreme heat the number one weather-related killer in the United States. Here's why something so quiet is so dangerous.

cards.headline: Your body's cooling system
cards.body: Your body cools itself by sweating: as sweat evaporates, it carries heat away. In humid air, sweat evaporates more slowly, so the cooling system stalls while the heat keeps coming. That's why forecasters give a heat index, what the temperature feels like once humidity is counted in. Sticky heat is harder on you than dry heat.

items.label: Heat exhaustion
points: Heavy sweating
Cold, pale, clammy skin
Fast, weak pulse
Move somewhere cool, loosen clothes, sip water

items.label: Heat stroke
points: Body temperature of 103°F or higher
Hot, red, dry or damp skin
Fast, strong pulse; confusion

cards.headline: Why cities run hotter
cards.body: Roofs, roads and parking lots soak up the Sun's heat and give it back, more than forests or lakes do. Cities also have fewer trees to shade the ground and release water from their leaves. The result is a heat island: in the US, about 1 to 7°F hotter than outlying areas by day and 2 to 5°F hotter at night, as the pavement slowly lets its stored heat go.

cards.headline: Who is most at risk
cards.body: Heat doesn't hit everyone equally. The National Weather Service lists infants and children, older adults (especially those with health conditions or living alone), people with chronic illnesses and pregnant women as the most vulnerable. That's why heat safety includes other people: check on older, sick or frail neighbors when a heat wave arrives.

title: Floods: Turn Around, Don't Drown
objective: After this level you can explain how flash floods form and why driving into floodwater is so dangerous.
summary: A flash flood begins within hours of heavy rain, fastest where water can't soak in. A foot of rushing water can carry away most cars, so Turn Around, Don't Drown.

cards.headline: Six inches of fast water can knock you off your feet.
cards.body: A flash flood can turn a quiet creek or a highway underpass into a torrent within hours. Here's how that happens, and why a car is the worst place to meet one.

cards.headline: What makes a flood flash
cards.body: A flash flood begins within 6 hours of heavy rain, often within 3, and the rain usually comes from thunderstorms. How fast it arrives depends on how hard it rains, the slope, the plants and how soggy the soil already is. It can even strike where it isn't raining: heavy rain upstream can turn your quiet creek into a torrent.

cards.headline: Where rain can't soak in
cards.body: In a forest, much of the rain soaks into the soil and trickles to streams slowly. A city swaps that sponge for roofs, roads and parking lots. The water can't sink in, so it races off and reaches the streams all at once. Same storm, faster flood: pavement makes floods more frequent and more severe.

cards.fact: It takes just 12 inches of rushing water to carry away most cars.
cards.context: Two feet carries off SUVs and trucks. Over half of flood drownings happen when someone drives into floodwater, and the road under that water may already have collapsed.

mascot.line: If you remember one thing from this level, make it this: Turn Around, Don't Drown. Floodwater is never worth the shortcut.

cards.headline: Turn Around, Don't Drown
cards.body: That's the rule from the National Weather Service and Ready.gov, and it's short on purpose. Never drive around the barriers on a flooded road. Never drive or walk into floodwater, however passable it looks. Turning around costs you a few minutes. It's the easiest safety decision you'll ever make.

title: Why Wildfires Spread
objective: After this level you can explain how heat, drought, wind and fuel combine to drive a wildfire and a longer fire season.
summary: Fire needs heat, oxygen and fuel; a wildfire's behavior depends on fuels, weather and slope. Western fire seasons are over a month longer, as warming meets fuel built up by suppression.

cards.headline: A wildfire usually runs faster uphill than down.
cards.body: Fire needs only three ingredients to start. How far and fast a wildfire spreads depends on three more. Learn both, and a fire forecast starts to make sense.

cards.headline: Two triangles
cards.body: The fire triangle is heat, oxygen and fuel: what any fire needs to burn. Firefighters add a second, the fire behavior triangle: fuels, weather and topography, the shape of the land. The first triangle says whether something burns. The second says how a wildfire will behave once it does.

cards.headline: Fuel, weather, slope
cards.body: In fuel, moisture matters most. Living trees hold a lot of water and dead logs very little, and a fire must drive the water off before anything burns. Wind feeds the flames fresh oxygen and pushes them toward new fuel. Low humidity dries fuel out, so it catches faster and burns faster. And a wildfire typically runs faster uphill than downhill or on flat ground.

cards.headline: A longer fire season
cards.body: Looking back over 35 years of weather data, Forest Service scientists found fire seasons starting earlier in spring and running later into autumn. Parts of the western US now have seasons more than a month longer. NASA points to two things working together: a warming climate (hotter weather, earlier snowmelt, warmer nights, less summer rain) and decades of fire suppression that let fuel pile up in some forests.

title: Paris and the Climate Debate
objective: After this level you can describe what the Paris Agreement aims for and the main options people argue over for cutting emissions and adapting.
summary: Paris aims for well below 2°C of warming, pursuing 1.5°C. Responses either cut emissions or adapt, and every option, from carbon pricing to geoengineering research, has supporters and critics.

cards.headline: In 2015, countries agreed on a goal. How to reach it is still argued.
cards.body: The goal is a number on a thermometer. The argument is about nearly everything else: what to change, who pays and what to try. Here's the goal, and the main options people weigh.

cards.headline: What Paris aims for
cards.body: The Paris Agreement was reached at the COP21 conference on 12 December 2015 and came into force on 4 November 2016. Its long-term goal: hold global warming to well below 2°C above pre-industrial levels, and pursue efforts to limit it to 1.5°C. It doesn't set one plan for everyone. Every five years, each country is expected to submit its own updated plan, called a nationally determined contribution.

cards.headline: Cut or cope?
cards.body: Responses come in two kinds. Mitigation cuts the flow of greenhouse gases, by burning less fossil fuel or by strengthening the natural sinks that store carbon, like forests, oceans and soil. Adaptation adjusts to the climate we have or expect, to lower risks such as rising seas and extreme weather. The Paris Agreement covers both.

items.label: Carbon pricing
points: Supporters: a cost-effective way to cut emissions
Critics: higher energy costs hit lower-income households harder
Supporters reply: return the money to those households

items.label: Nuclear power

cards.headline: Dimming the sunlight?
cards.body: The most debated idea copies a volcano: spray fine particles into the stratosphere to reflect sunlight. NOAA notes it could cool the planet faster than removing carbon dioxide, but it does nothing about the greenhouse gases building up, and the GAO notes its side effects, on rainfall and the ozone layer for example, are poorly understood. A 2021 National Academies report backed research, while calling emission cuts and adaptation the first line of defense.

title: Myths About Weather and Climate
objective: After this level you can spot and correct common mix-ups, from the ozone hole causing warming to a cold snap disproving it.
summary: Three common mix-ups, corrected: the ozone hole isn't what's warming Earth, one cold week is weather, not climate, and humans emit far more CO2 than volcanoes.

cards.headline: Humans emit at least 60 times as much CO2 as all the world's volcanoes.
cards.body: Yet "it's really the volcanoes" is a claim you'll hear. So are two others. Here are three common mix-ups, and the evidence that fixes each one.

cards.headline: Myth: the ozone hole is warming the planet
cards.body: It sounds logical: a hole in the sky lets in more sunlight. But what the ozone hole lets through is extra ultraviolet light, and NASA says that can't explain the warming of Earth's surface. The ozone hole's role in global warming is small compared with the impacts of other human activities. Two real problems; don't swap their causes.

cards.headline: Myth: a cold snap disproves warming
cards.body: You met weather versus climate in World Geography. Climate is a long-term average, often taken over 30 years; weather changes by the hour. Earth has warmed over the past century or so, but that doesn't mean it never gets cold. Blizzards and hard freezes still happen each winter; they're just likely to come less often. One cold week proves nothing either way.

mascot.line: This is Level 1's volcano again. Big eruptions nudge Earth's thermostat down, not up.

cards.fact: People emit 60 or more times as much carbon dioxide each year as volcanoes.
cards.context: And the carbon dioxide from today's eruptions has never caused detectable global warming. Their sulfur dioxide has done the opposite, occasionally cooling the planet in a way instruments can detect.
